common thief, a confederate of Carson's, one of a gang of sharpers, aye, the chief of the gang. And to such a man she had bound herself for life. She could never leave him. His life must be her life. She was wedded to a swindler, who had already paid the penalty of one crime, and was wanted for another. The police were on his track. Carson had said as much.

"Amy." said Athelstane, in a low voice. But she drew the silk coverlet over her head, and refused to hear him. Strangely enough, she never thought of upbraiding the man who had so cruelly deceived her. Like all women, she took the blame upon herself. • Surely she ought to have, known better. Had not her parents warned her? Had she not rushed into the marriage blindly, against all advice?
"Amy," said Athelstane again. "I loved you, Dick,"- Was all she could reply. Her sobs choked utterance. Her whole body trembled. For evermore misery and fear would haunt her. -
But though he had wronged her, Athelstane had his better side. He was pot so unprincipled as his confederate.

"Amy," he said, softly, "it is all true. There are dark spots in my past. I dared not tell you about them. But the love I gave you was strong and deep. I loved you for yourself, and you redeemed me. I tried to break away from the old set,' and begin a new life along with you. I thought I had succeeded, but last week Carson found me out. He's not such a bad sort, Amy. You'll like him after a bit. He-"
But she at up in-bed with flaming eyes, "Has he gone ? " she demanded. ..__ __

"Yes." - "Then see that he never comes here again." "Certainly, dear." Athelstane gave the promise without a moment's hesitation. Be meant to keep it, too. Bringing all his powers to the task, he won her over. He was devoted to her, he said. She had lifted him from the mire of his old self and set him on his feet again. His conduct had been faultless since he met her. Had he not shewn himself the best of husbands? Had he not indulged her in every way? Let her ask what she liked, if London could supply it it should be hers.

Va. the one thing Amy wanted London could not supply. Even its boundless resources were of no avail. In which of its shops or warehouses could she buy back her peace of mind, repurchase happi- ness? It was impossible. Yet no sooner did she realise the peril in which her husband stood than ter heart opened to Wm. He was in danger of being arrested any moment. In sympathetic courage her own wounds were forgotten. Was it not through her influence that Dick had forsaken his old ways? Yes, he had/done everything for her. She would not fail him in the hour of need. It was monstrous to think he would be captured, put in a prison cell, just when, for her sake, he had turned over a new leaf. No, she would be true, she would not desert him.

And so he won her over, persuaded her gentle heart, bewitched her by the glamour of his love. They kissed in tears. Till death they would be faithful. Only there was one thing. Carson must not come to the house again. But Carson insisted upon coming. He came that very evening, in fact. All Athelstane's entreaties could not prevent him. The scamp had been struck with Amy. He would not keep away, and he held her husband in his power. They were forced to admit him.

He was shewn into the dining-room by his chief. Helping himself to a glass of brandy, Carson insisted that Mrs. Athelstane should come down. Amy refused. Once her husband came to her room and intimated his friend's wish. She would not hear of it. Returning to the dining-room Athelstane begged his confederate to desist. "Hang it all, cried Carson. "What does she take me for? If you're good enough for her, Dick, what right has she to turn up her nose at me?" "Women are women, Bob," said Athelstane, trying to pacify him. "You gave her a scare this afternoon. Have patience; she'll come round all right. We can't make her like you just at once, you know." "You can't ? " roared Carson. "Then, by Heaven, I will I"

He made two steps towards the dining-room door, but Athelstane stood in his way. A crisis had come. Carson, indeed, had him in his power. A word from him would consign Amy's husband to Wormwood Scrubbs. Nevertheless, Athelstane turned the lock, pulled out the key, and slipped it into his breast-pocket. Folding his arms across it, he looked his accomplice straight in the face. "Now, Bob," he said, emphatically, "don't be a fool. If she declines to see you, that's an end of it. I can't have you coming here and making scenes."
"Scenes! By Jove! but there will be scenes. What the mischief does the minx mean by refusing to see me?"

"She's not obliged to see you or anyone except myself, is she?" 'And what better right have you to the girl than all the rest of us ? ' cried Carson, beside him- self with rage. "Don't you belong to the set' Weren't we to go shares in everything?" Athelstane cursed the past; but, if possible, he must not quarrel with this man. They had been band and glove irr too many deeds of darkness. "Now, Bob," he said, "sit down and shew yourself a bit reasonable. I've done all I can for you, and if Amy won't come down she shan't be forced."

"Shan't she ? " Carson growled. He dropped into a chair, however, and accepted the glass of cjiampagne which Athelstane poured out. The latter hoped that the worst was over, and that he would get rid of the intruder. But, thief against thief! Cunning against cunning! Both men began to drink. Carson lit a cigar. Presently he was laughing and talking about sporting matters, and seemed to have quite forgotten the object of his visit. Athelstane encouraged the mood. He continued to ply him with wine. Once, twice, thrice, he crossed to the sideboard for a fresh bottle. It was a magnificent oak sideboard, with a superb plate-glass mirror at the back. The fourth time Athelstane advanced to it to his horror he saw a man rush up behind, Before he could turn Carson had him by the throat. There was a sharp struggle. Each was a man in the prime of life. Bursting from the grasp of his assailant, Amy's husband faced round, closed with him, and tried to force him to the floor.

Backwards and forwards they struggled. Cloth- ing was torn, chairs were overturned; there was a crash which could be heard all over the house, as the combatants dropped on the carpet. The servants came rushing to the door, so did poor Amy. They knocked, they shoutod, they implored, but all in vain. The two menrwere locked in the death-grapple, and the door would not yield. "Now, Carson, if I let you rise you will leave the house at once ? "

Athelstane was uppermost. He had his accom- plice by the throat, his knee was on his chest. "Suppose so, Dick. You've got the best of it." "And you'll promise not to come back here and bother my wife again?" There was a moment before Carson answered. "Promise" said Amy's husband, tightening his grip. "Yes, Dick."

Athelstane let go. With the breath almost 'knocked out of his body, Carson got to his feet. "Brandy!" he panted. His host poured out a glass. Swallowing it at a gulp, Carson steadied himself against the table. "Rather rough on an old pal, Dick," he said, opening the buttons of his coat. For reply Athelstane pointed to the door. He could hear his wife sobbing without. The thing must be ended at once. Carson had come to the same conclusion. The thing must. be ended, But it was to end far differently from what Athelstane expected. His confederate had been unbuttoning his coat and vest. To breathe more freely, Athelstane supposed. But suddenly Carson dived into the recesses of his attir4and whipped out a revolver. The chief was at, his mercy. "Now," said the Scamp, pulling back the trigger, "you've stolen a march on me, Bic run away from the set,' and married the only girl whom I have ever have loved. Yes, by Heaven! I love her! She has got to be mine—mine, I tell you. Will you give her lip? " The steel barrel gleamed in ,Athelaane's face. There was no answer to such an - argument. But Amy was weeping outside the door. He knew that she loved him. Had she not given a signal proof of her affection only two hours ago? Surrender her to Carson? 'J2o a man she loathed? To the wretch who had wrecked their happiness? Never! "Do you call this fair, Bob?" he asked, slowly. "All's fair in love, they say," Carsori replied, with his cynical smile. "I could have strangled you a moment ago,' said At hlestane.,
"And a precious fool you were not to do it. Now it's my turn. For the second time, will you give her up? " "No!"
Folding his arms and keeping his face towardit his antagonist Athelstane retreated step by step to the door. He set his back against it.

Black Petticoats.—The black silk gown that is past its hour of triumph should first be utilised as a founda- tion for some transparent material, then a semi-trans- parent fabric, and last of all turned into a petticoat— upon which divers flounces can be buttoned. For out- door wear there is nothing more modish- that a black silk petticoat which looks well with any toilette. The flounce—where economy has to be studied—should be lined, and simply gathered into the band. The accordion pleated flounces sold ready to button on,are dainty and fascinating, but their term of usefulness. is brief in the extreme.

div.head: WOMEN'S CHAT.
div.p: WOMEN'S CHAT.

It will be a sad blow to the peasants of Normandy and Brittany when they realise that misletoe is going out of fashion, and all the market authorities agree that there has been much less .demand for the white berried plant this year. Most of it conies from the French ports, and a large number of Bretons look to the gin" harvest to pay the rent Some few years ago the French Government ordered the destruction of the parasite in all the orchards, but the peasants do not believe that it injures the apple trees, and instead of destroyinr, it, they cultivate the plant as much as ever. They will, however, have to look for other means to pay the winter's rent, if misletoe is to be no longer used for the Christmas enlivenmmt of British homes. .

Christmas Warnings.—li is the custom of the medical journals to take a doleful view of the approach of Christmas. There was a slight exception last year when one of them did acknowledge that plum pudding was not after all such a deadly compound, and that, eaten in not undue quantities, it was even good and nourish- ing food. But as a rule these journals are so full of warnings with regard to Christmas fare, -and Yuletide celebrations, that it is a wonder that some of us survive these suspected dangers. One, to which our attention is directed, is however the very real one of the danger of fire from domestic theatricals, and the perilous custont'of dressing up young people in cotton-wool to represent Father \Christmas, er other snow covered characters. Once this catches fire—and usually there are many lighted candles about on such occasions— there is the greatest risk of the victim being burnt to death. There is also an increased risk of fire now that so many toys and orivients are made of celluloid, and those who are organising juvenile parties cannot be too careful to keep these articles away from the coloured candles on the Christmas tree.

The, Fire Fiend.—The Christmas arrangenients of the Royal Family camelvery near to being upset by thetalarm- ing outbreak of fire at Sandringham, but happily that occurrence has inno way interfered with their Majesties' plans for spending Yuletide as usual at their Norfolk seat. It is no doubt some satisfaction to their Majesties to know that the fire was not caused by any accident to the electric lighting arrangements. Had that been the fire, the fear of re, which is an ever present one in great houses, would be more a terror than ever, but the outbreak seems to have been due to the very common cause of beams not sufficiently protected against flues or firegrates. This has caused the destruction of hundreds of old country houses, and has on more than one occasion been the cause of fires at Windsor Castle. At the same time, it is surprising that such negligence should be found at Sandringham, as it is quite a modern building, and after the great fire there some twelve years ago, which destroyed nearly all of the upper rooms, not only was the re-building carried out upon. Ereproof principles, but the whole structure was over- hauled with a view to minimising the danger from fire. Improved Sanitation.—Another source of danger which used to exist in the Royal Palaces and many old country houses,—that arising from imperfect drainage —has been practically eliminated by modern methods of sanitation. In this we have made more progress than have other countries, and it is stillPsaid that the palaces of the Czar are veritable plague spots on account of theiedefective drainage. In recent years, the drainage at Windsor Caale, and of practically all the Royal resi- dences, has been wholly re-constructed, and it is an understood condition that such work has been carried out before the King pays a visit to any of the country houses of the great and wealthy. Byer since the King contracted typhoid fever in a Yorkshire mansion, in 1871, the greatest care is taken to ensure that there is "nothing wrong with the drains" before his Majesty goes on a country house visit. Must Live in the Country.—The last Sir John Blundell Maple made it- a condition in his will that his daughter the Baroness von Eckhardstein should reside for 2-10 days each year in the United Kingdors, if she is to enjoy the large income bequeathed to her by her father. Most people would no doubt be prepared to live 340 days each year in this country for half the money. but, at the same time it is a singular condition as Baron Eckhardstein is a distinguished member of the German diplomatic service and might be called upon to fill some high post in Berlin. Fortunately for the Baroness, the trustees of the late Sir J. Blundell Maple, have power to modify this.condit ion,. so that no difficulty is likely to arise should it become desirable for her to live abroad for her health, or for her husband to give up his residence in this country. But speaking generally such conditions are undesirable in a will, as the testator cannot foresee circumstances which may make the effect of their action the very opposite to that they intended. Fashionable Jewellery.—The superstition against the opal dies hard, but this Yuletide jewellers report a fair demand for the so-called unlucky-stone. Another gem in great favour is the Scotch pearl, which differs from the Oriental in that it suggests the rainbow shades of the opal, but possesses none of the exquisite sheen of the Oriental pearls. The Duchess of Portland and the Duchess of Sutherland both possess some very fine ornaments composed of Scotch pearls, which owing to the fact that it is unusual to find many of the same , size and shape, are very valuable, and much sought after. Yet another stone in considerable request is the tourmaline. In colour it is between emerald and olivine, and appears at its best when set with diamonds or pearls. The topaz, set with diamonds, is being much 'Worn too by modish women, the firshion being set by her Majesty the Queen, who has donned upon several occasions recently, some very magnificeat ornaments composed of these particular stones. A Useful Idert.—A thin-necked woman 'always seems possessed of the notion that for her a low cut evening -bodice is an impossibility. But there is a way of overcom- ing the difficulty of hiding away unsightly collar bones.a vrayboth easy and economical.A collar band of lace,with deep vandykes of lace pointing downwards, and so arranged as to cover the prominent bones in front and the hollowness on either side, is all that is needed, and These vandykes should meet and be fastened to a round dikolletage, which conveys an impression of roundness i wanting n the square or V shape, oncerso modish. -Into the lace collar band and vandykes, jewelled brooches, Scc., may be pinned, when the effect will be

div.p: STOCKTON HEATH.

ST. THOM AS'S CHURCH.—On Saturday afternoon the annual Christmas tree and Sale of Work was opened in the Church Institute. There was a very large attendance at the opening ceremony, when the Rev. H. V. Pigot. vicar, presided. In calling upon Miss Wilson to declare the sale open the Chairman said they were very dis- appointed that Mrs. Vere Davies was unable to attend, but they had an excellent substitute in Miss Wilson—a lady who had taken the greatest interest in those sales and in their preparation. (Applause.) Miss Wilson then declared the sale open, and wished it every success On the proposition of the Chairman, seconded by the Rev: C. A. M. Evans, a vote of thanks was accorded to IWissWilsonand the sale of goods was then proceeded with After payment of expenses, the proceeds amounted to over £l6. This sun is divided equally between the S.P.G. and the Church of England Waifs and Strays' Society.

UNITED BAND OF HOPE MEETING.—On Monday evening the third monthly public meeting of Hill Cliffe and Stockton Heath Band of Hope Union was held in Providence schoolroom, under the presidency of the Rev. G. S. Hughes. There was a crowded attendance including the Rev. G. H. Carnson, Mr. Joseph Owen,and Mr. G. Whitfield (secretary.) An excellent programme was given by the members. Songs were contributed by the Misses C. Kenwerthy, H. Burgess, and May Isherwood, and Master Harry Moores, and recitations by May ;Vernon, Elsie Whitfield, - Daisy Burgess, Lilly Powell, Annie Broadhurst,Mary Earle, and Alice Cliffe, and Masters Arthur Whitfield,, W. Rustage, A. Burgess, Albert Bailey, and Harold Jones. The dialogue "Ten little temperance boys," by small boys, was well given, as was also the "Three little temperance girls," by 'Morrie Powell and Edith ,and Maud Kirkland. Other dialogues were : " What spoiled Christmas," by Mary Owen and Evelyn Beck; " Fret Saws v. Cigarettes," by Sanley Jones and George Andrews ; and a humorous dialogue," Rather provoking," by Misses Florrie Lowe and Lillian Hall, and Masters A. Whitfield, J. Whitfield and Reg. Miller. The Rev. G. H. Carnson delivered an address in which he secured the interest andattention 'of both children and adults. He appealed to the chil- dren to be trustworthy, in earnest, to form good resolutions,and to remain firm to the pledge. Mr. Joseph Owen, the speaker appointed by the Warrington Baud of Hope Union, gave and address pointing out the ntany advantages of being members of the Band of Hope. The Misses Woods and Jones and Master Whitfield acted as accompanists.

RUNCORN _PETTY SESSIONS

At these sessions, on 'Monday, before Mr. E. J. Nor- man and J. Pritchard. Owen Morris,. James Smith and John Grey, Weston Point, were summoned for using obscene/language at Weston Point, on December 6th, Grey pleaded guilty and the others not guilty. After hearing the evidence the magistrates fined Grey 10s. and the two others were discharged.—Bridget O'Neil,Heath- road, Runcorn, was fined 10s. on the evidence of P.C. Preston for using obscene language in Heath-road on December sth. William Goulding, St. Helens, was charged with having stolen or received, with a know- ledge that they had been stolen, 100 cigars belonging to James Tatlock, licensee of the Holyhead Arms public- house. The evidence was that the defendant and another man, who was sent to gaol last week for being concerned in the theft, went into the public-house and while the servant was away from the bar took a box of cigars. A ticket collector at Runcorn Bridge noticed that Goulding had a cigar box under his coat. Detec- tive Mottershead received the prisoner from the St.. Helens police and charged him with having stolen the cigars. He r6lied : I don't plead guilty to stealing them, but cannot say about receiving them as I was drunk at the time." Prisoner said he met the other man casually and left him in Widnes. There were 2:1 previous convictions and prisoner was committed to gaol for two months.

div.head: Examiner Saturday, December 19, 1903.
div.p: The Examiner Saturday, December 19, 1903.
FASHIONS OF TO-DAY.

There is great variety in regard to hair- dressing this season, and no particular style predominates markedly, over the others. People seem to follow the sensible plan of arranging their hair in as becoming a style as possible to suit themselves individually, although, of course, when out-of-doors the hat to be worn has to be considered and one's tressel arranged accordingly The fashion for having the hair softly waved and drawn up to the top of the head with very little fulness at the back and a deep-puffed wave across the forehead is a pretty one, and is very generally adopted for out-of-doors. It has the advantage of keeping in smoother and better order than that dressed low, as in the latter case the rubbing of the fur necklet or coat-collar is sure to disarrange the taste- fully-arranged knot. A small tortoiseshell clasp or brooch studded with green or blue stones is used to keep the short hairs at the back of the neck in order, while a larger comb

div.head: OIFFURE
div.p: OIFFURE
A STYLI

to match is thrust through the hair further up. The newest style of combs are sold in sets of three—two for the sides and one for the back—and are the colour of old -ivory Set with coloured stones and gilt. They are exceedingly smart-looking, and at present have not ~deteriorised by. general adoption. Nothing, however, looks so well for evening dress as the hair dressed in the manner depicted, with the twisted knot low on the neck, while the front of the hair is raised high in the Pompadour fashion.

-When the hair- is dressed in this fashion ornamental combs are a necessity, as they push the fulness out at the sides and hold it in place. Large Alsatian bows are some- times worn in the hair when it is dressed on the top of the head, the colour of the bows either emphasising that of the toilette or striking a charming- note of contrast. A black lace gown worn with Gloire-de-Dijon roses at .the breast looks all the better for a yellow bow in the hair; while I have seen and admired the fascinating effect of a crim-

ANTI' BLOUSE. son bow worn with a pale yellow toilette by a richly-complexioned brunette. Sparkling sequins or tiny iridescent beads are very effective when sewn on these coquettish bows, and black cut jet and sparkling sequins look particularly well on a black bow perched on blonde tresses. Empire wreaths of roses also look well, and are becom- ing to young faces, but somehow seem out of place in conjunction with a complexion which has lost its first freshness and bloom.

The dainty blouse sketched is of a simple yet charming . style. It is made of soft Oriental satin tucked all over, while some soft lace is draped across the shoulders from the centre of the back, where it forms a V. and brought to either side of the decolletage. The interval across the front is finished by soft swa things of chiffon arranged in a chou in the centre. The sleeves are also of tucked satin, fitting closely to the elbow, after which the satin is puffed, and then finishes in a deep lace frill. An old bodice could be smarted up by arranging it in a similar style, utilising any old good lace such as many of us have. treasured as lovely but somewhat useless heirlooms. One can do almost anything

AN AFTERNOON BLOUSE. with an old lace shawl or scarf in the way of decorating an evening toilette or cloak, or enhancing a tea-gown.. Great care should be Itaken in tacking the lace in place not to injure it in any way, as darns, however care- fully and neatly dope, lessen the value of the , lace.

It is wonderful how carefully our grand- mothers preserved these dainty laces, while one set of firrs lasted a lifetime. Nowadays a woman seems to want • a new set each winter ; such is the extravagance of the present day. My last sketch shows a smart blouse for afternoon wear. It is made of fine flannel, and is trimmed, with an edging of coarse lace. The front is also covered with lace ,to match, and the blouse fastens down the side underneath one of the revers. , It is difficult nowadays to distinguish between a bodice and a blouse, for. the latter is no longer a loose unlined garment, but must be carefully cut and fitted to the figure of the wearer if ,success is to be ensured. The colour also .must match as nearly as possible that of the skirt, or at least harmonise with it. Now that Christmas is not far off the shops are out-rivalling each other' by displaying the most fascinating goods and garments. There are many charming silk and satin slip's trimmed with lace and insertion, which may be counted on as presents welcomed by every girl, for they are for the most part well cut- and daintily made, and can be worn over a tight-iitting slip. Stock collars of lace and lawn and dainty cravats and bows there are in plenitude, while the hundred- and-one trifles which complete a toilette are more fascinating this year than before.
COQUETTE.

div.head: AMY REDFERN'S ORDEAL.
div.p: AMY REDFERN'S ORDEAL.
By G. E. MANSFIELD. Author of "Rebecca," "Lost Souls," "Red Star," "In One Time," &c,

Both her father and young 'Tark Somerville, who had loved her all his life, cod what they could to dissuade her. But Amy, dazzled by Atlaelstane's showy style, struck with his handsOme figure, and captivated by the story of his wonderful career, married the adventurer, and went to live with him at 2.3, Buckingham Circus. He had furnished superb apartments, and for three months her dreary was unbroken. She herself was only twenty-one, bright, wilful, and vivacious, with all the deepet elements of her nature still undeveloped. And to her the hero was a god. No man could be mote attractive, none more courteous, none more devoted to his bride. West End society threw its doors wide open. Young Mr. and Mrs. Athelstane were wanted everywhere. No dinner, no supper- party, no rout could be complete without them. For three months it lasted, then the bubble burst.

It was a Wednesday afternoon, and Amy was sitting alone in her drawing-room, when the foot- man shewed up a dark, uncouth individual, whom she had never met before. The stranger had not announced himself by any card, so the young wife had no clue to his identity. Yet the man,• a short, square-built person with cynical eyes, made himself pile at home, and seemed to know the house.

"Where's the boss, Joe?" he' asked the foot- man, giving him a pinch. "Master's out," the man replied. "So! Is he now? And -who's this pretty butterfly he has got here? " The footman tittered. Mrs. Athelstane looked indignantly at the intruder. "Do you know the gentleman, Joseph?" she asked the servant.

"Bob Carson, my dear,"inswered the stranger himself, advancing to the settee where Amy had been sitting. Instinctively slit drew back. There was something about the man which made her loathe him from the first.

"Mr. Athelstane will return at seven," she said, politely. "Can I do anything for you? I am his wife." "Wife!" shouted Carson, looking a the foot- man. The litter grinned, and nodded an assent. "His wife! The boss married! 'Whew!"

Thrusting both hands into his trousers, and stretching his feet apart, Mr. Carson screwed his mouth into a whistle, and gazed at Amy, as though she were a Zoological curiosity. His hat, which he had not troubled to remove, was stuck on the back of his head in a rakish manner. The smell of tobacco and a strong odour or recent brandies had filled the room since his arrival. What could such a man want with the refined Richard Athelstane ?

Amy returned his gaze. She looked him full in the face. Her cheeks tingled; her eyes flashed fire. Oh! had she been a man. Impertinence would hare spun through the bow-window into the street below. Mocked in her own house, insulted before a servant, Mrs. Athelstane returned the gaze of the intruder with all the outraged dignity of a well- bred Englishwoman., • And Carson felt her power—by degrees came under her spell. As his eyes drank in her beauty and the wonderful grace of her fine style, his sottish expression changed. He knew he was in the presence of a lady. His feet drew themselves together, the rascal raised his hat, and murmured something apologetic for his intrusion. But Amy was fully roused. Perceiving that she had the ascendancy, she determined to make use of it. Her tone was frigid, and her jewelled finger pointed to the door, as she said: "You will please leave the house, sir."
' Her pride and the deserved scorn which she poured on him awoke the fiend in Carson. A moment before, he was repentant, shamed. Now he became defiant.
"What do you take. me for ?" he asked, ironically.

"A tipsy man," said Mrs. Athelstane. "I'm master in this house, by Jove! And I'll let you and your swell husband know it. Order me out, will you? Here, Joe! Take my hat and coat. I guess I'll wait till Dick comes back." Tossing his things to the footman, Mr. Carson threw himself on to an ottoman, and snapped his fingers in Amy's face. He was quite himself again. His head was clear, his strength collected. Ife had realised the situation at once. This woman had come between him and his confederate. That was why Athelstane had vanished from the "set." This woman was his idol. Carson felt himself supplanted. Moreover, she had thrown down the gage of battle. She had ordered him out of the house. The challenge had transformed him. He was drunk no longer. She would find a formidable antagonist. If she played "the lady with him, he, Carson, would confront her in his old shape, as a polished scamp. The tables were turned. Amy's quick brain told her this immediately. She had mistaken the man. However low Carson had fallen„ he was no boor who sat before her, but her equal in birth and culture, and in will-power more than her match. But she was not going to surrender without a struggle. "What is the meaning of this ? " she managed to ask. "This is my house. You have insulted me. You shall answer for it as soon as my husband returns."

As though summoned by her necessity, the drawing-room door flew open at that instant, and Athelstane appeared. But no longer the serene, the self-reliant Athelstane, no longer the strong man of talent. Her husband hung his head as he shuffled into the room.
"Well, Dick, old boy! Wot cheer?" said hie 'confederate. His cynical eyes twinkled at the chief's discomfiture.

"Hang it!" muttered Athelstane. "I thought you were to go to the club, Bob ? " "Come now, Dick. Make a fellow welcome, can't you? You're not going to keep the pretty butterfly all to yourself? ' "Do you know this gentleman. Richard ? asked the unfortunate wife. A terrible misgiving had risen in her heart. - "Know me?" cried Carson. "Should rather think he does. Know me? Why, that is a joke. Haven't we been pals for fifteen years ? Didn't we do five-"

"I say, Bob," interrupted Athelstane, "cow and see me in the dining-room, will you? There's a decent chap." Her husband was terribly perturbed. He was deadly pale. His teeth rattled, and his limbs trembled. Amy could scarcely believe that it was the same man who stood before her. But Carson had been insulted. Mrs. Athelstane had ordered him out of the house. He was deter- mined to humiliate her. Crossing one knee over the Other, he shook his head to his accomplice, and refused to budge. "Sit down, Dick," he said, maliciously. "Not taken the wife into your confidence yet, eh, my boy ? " ."For Heaven's sake, Richard, who is this gentle- man?" Amy asked. again. "Is he a friend of yours? " "Best friend old Dick has got, my dear," said Carson, waving him to be silent. "If I had not come here this afternoon, your hubty would have had the derbies 'on his wrists to-night. Fact, Dick. The club has been suspected. Heard it just in the nick of time to-day. We were all to be nabbed at Old Compton-street to-night. That Park Lane job! Would have been another five fears for both of us. Now, Mrs. Athelstane, perhaps you will be civil, and shake hands with your husband's best friend."

There was a long, sad moan from a woman's heart. Athelstane glowered at his accomplice. A curse rose to his lips. "Sst, Dick," said Carson, as he watched the poison working. And it worked rapidly. There was a cry, a crash. Both men sprang to their feet. Amy bad fallen to the floor between them.
When she regained consciousness, she found herself lying in her own room. Athelstane stood by the bedside, but she turned her face to the wall. fThe could not bear to look at him.

The blow had been so swift, so tcrr;hle. That morning her husband had seemed to Ler the one man in the universe. For him she had left a com- fortable home: for him she had turned her back on young Mark Somerville, who, in a thousand ways, had shown that he cared for her. Trusting with all the ardour of her one-and-twenty. years, she had loved Athels!ane as few men have becn loved. In him she had found her maiden's ideal, the cne man on earth whom she could worship !vial all her heart. And now disillusionment had come. He who had bewitched her with his talk, he who had wooed and won her, he with whom she had stood at the altar only thrce months ago and taken the vows which are irrevocable, was a

' "Shoot!" he said. Carson took deliberate aim. One click, one bullet, and Amy would be his. Yet the weapon fell from his hand:— It dropped upon the table. "Hang it, Dick," he called, "I can't do it. We've been pals for fifteen years, and you were deuced decent when you had me down. Tell you what, we'll cut for the girl. There's a pack of cards there on the mantlepiece. Only one can have her; lowest wins."

A born gamester, Athelstane accepted the offer. He scarcely knew what he was doing; but many a time fortune had befriended him; she would not fail him now. The cards were laid on the table. "Lowest wins," Carson repeated, stretching out his hand.
"Three of spades! By Jove! she's mine, Dick."
Atheist ane cut.
"Three of hearts!" he cried, triumphantly. But a cold sweat broke over him. If it had been one point less? Carson put. forth his hand again. _ _ .

"Hang it!" he cried. "A fen." Although the chance was more in his own favour Athelstane shook as he turned his card. His face was like a corpse. "Queen!" shouted Carson, bringing his fist down upon the table with a thump. "Mine! Mine! I've won her. Hullo--"
For there was a flash, a loud report. Lifting the revolver from the table Athelstane had placed the muzzle behind his ear and fired. Death was instantaneous.

Carson was thunderstruck. Two minutes, three minutes, four minutes, he stood there motionless, his eyes riveted upon the dead body lying on the. carpet. He heard not the clamour at the door. He knew not that a ladder had been raised to the window, and that two constables had their hands upon the sash. Admiration and remorse were struggling within him. "Bravo, Dick!" he said, at length. "Game to the end. Ido believe he loved her." There was a clang. The 'door fell from its hinges. From the landing and by the window twenty constables; led by young Mark Somerville, burst into the room.
[DIE END.

div.head: CARTER'S SERIOUS ACCIDENT.
div.p: A CARTER'S SERIOUS ACCIDENT.
Unsuccessful Compensation Claiill at Warrington.

• At the Warrington County Court on Thursday,before his Honour Judge Bowen Rowlands, K.C., Thomas HOgett, 4, Russell-street, brought an action under the Employers' Liability Act against John Barlow, coal dealer, 253, Winwicii-road, to recover £2[4 10s. com- pensation for injuries sustained by the wheel of a lurry passing over him whilst in the defendant's employ. The accident, it was submitted, happened in conse- quence of the vice of the horse which was harnessed to the lurry. Mr. F. Cuthbert Smith, barrister (instructed b y Nr.T. S. Steel) appeared for the plaintiff and Mr. Adshead Elliott (instructed by Mr. A. J. Willett) defended.

In opening the case, Mr. Cuthbert Smith said the plaintiff was employed by the defendant as a carter. Defendant bought the coal business from a Mr. Griffiths who previously employed the plaintiff, and the horse which, it was alleged, was the cause of the accident,was transferred with the business. When it was owned by Mr. Griffiths the animal had not developed vice to any great extent, although occasionally it had shown un- pleasant signs. It was not, however, really dangerous. When it was sold to the defendant the horse began to develop symptoms of a very marked character, the worst being that it would start off suddenly w.ithout any orders. Defendant was aware of the vice of the animal because on several occasions it had bolted away when he had been present. On Monday morning, May 25th, plaintiff harnessed the horse and took it to Messrs. Richardson's wharf for the purpose of loading coal into bags. The horse seemed to have got down to the siding in - record time and on arriving there plaintiff proceeded to load the 'cart. A man named Birch assisted by shovelling the coal into bags. Twice the animal started away and plaintiff did his best to stop it. Later on as they were finishing loading the coal an empty bag fell to the ground. Hodgett got off the lurry to pick it up and the horse started off. He called to it to stop, but without avail, and the top of the lurry caught plaintiff and knocked him to the ground. Two of the wheels passed over his stomach and he was badly hurt. He sustained spinal injuries, and also suffered from neuresthenia and chronic peritonitis. He was an in-patient of the Infirmary for about eight weeks. He was then discharged, but after being out a short time it was found absolutely neces- sary for him to re-enter the institution. lie was still] an in-patient, and had only seen allowed out that day for the purposes of the case. His injuries were extremely serious and it was doubtful whether he would be able to work again. Whilst in defendant's employ plaintiff earned £1 is. 6d. per week. On June 15th he wrote to the defendant asking for compensa- tion but received no reply. When the notice under the Employers' Liability Act was sent to the defendant by Mr. Steel he said "Your man is entitled to compensa- tion, I hope he will get it. It doesn't matter to me as lam insured." He never suggested that he was not liable.

Plaintiff gave evidence bearing out this statement. In cross-examination he denied that he had taught the horse certain tricks, including that of pick- ing up his coat from the ground. He never said that it would make a good circus horse and that it "could do anything but talk." He never pretended to put his head into the animal's mouth, and he had not allowed his children to play with the horse. He told defendant that it was not safe nine or ten months ago. He denied that he leaned over the lurry to pickup the bag and fell off. He did not start the horse. Dr. Hodkinson, senior house surgeon at the Infirmary said the plaintiff was suffering from chronic peritonitis, neuristhenia, and an injury to the spine in consequence of the accident.' He could not say when plaintiff would be able to return to work.

Martin Ward, a labourer formerly employed by Messrs Richardson, said ho had seen the horse start off sud- denly. It was on Monday mornings that this generally happened. Patrick Ward gave similar evidence.

'Mr. Sumner, clerk to Mr. Steel, said .he served the notice on the defendant who after reading it said he w4uld sign the acknowledgment with pleasure. Hodgett, he added, was entitled to compensation and he hoped he would get it. It did not matter much to him as he was insured.

Mr. Elliott said it was quite possible that defendant was under the impression that, the plaintiff was entitled to compensation under the Workmen's Compensation Act. Whatever defendrnt had said did not alter the position of affairs as he had made no admission of neg- ligence. It was necessary for the plaintiff to prove that the horse was of a vicious nature and that de- fendant was aware of the fact. In regard to the history of the horse during the past, seven or eight years he would call evidence of such a character that he was sure his friend wouldenvy the horse. (Laughter.) Pro- bably no one in the court, with the exception of his honour, would be able to bring such witnesses as to character as he would produce. (Laughter.) Never on a single occasion had Mr. tf,ri tUths seen the ;horse start unexpectedly and plaintiff had never complained to him about it. Plaintiff had not complained to Mr. Barlow who would state that the animal was a very quiet one Hodgett treated it as a pat. He (Mr. Elliott) ventured to say that the contention as to the viciousness of the horse was a fabrication. The accident did not come within the provisions of the Workmen's Compensation Act and therefore to make a special effort to obtain damages the story of the vicious nature of the horse was brought into being. Defendant was called and said that at one time he contemplated sending the horse to Knutsford where his son was in business. Plaintiff appealed to him so strongly not to send the horse that he decidednot to do so. It was as quiet a horse as there was in Warrington and witness had never seen it start unawares. Hodgett had never complained to him about it. He had seen plaintiff's children playing about the . horse in the stable Pond when he remonstrated with the plaintiff altent it he said it was too quiet to hurt them. Without hearing further evidence. his Honour, with gr:ett reluctance, decided in favour of the defendant. Plaintiff had to establish certain propositions but had failed to do so to his satisfaction. He had grave doubts as to whether the horse, excepting under special cir- cumstances, was apt to display such qualities as to be called a vicions horse. The second element of doubt was whether, if any such fault existed, defendant was never told about it. It was .undisputed that for two years and a half the plaintiff drove the horse fot GrifilthS without any complaint and that for a year or so he drove it for the defendant without co, plumping. It Was strange that a horse with such good behaviour for so long, should de- velop a habit of starting unawares so as to make it a vicious horse wi+lain the, legal r eaning of the phrase. If that was the case he was not satisfiel that defendant knew it. Another point was that if the horse was as vicious as plaintiff sought to make out, he was. not sure that Hodgett was not guilty of a deriliction of duty in getting down to p'ck no the !bag and leaving the horse unattended. I and every person -in the Court must feel for the plaintiff in his serious injuries but one must not allow svrnpathetic,coitsiderations to weigh with one in deciding the case. With eft) greatest possible reluctance he gave judgment for the cL;fendant without costs.

div.head: MOTHER OF TWENTY-SEVEN CHILDREN
div.p: MOTHER OF TWENTY-SEVEN CHILDREN

A Hindley WCII.IOII named Fitzgerald represented her son at Wigan County Court on Tuesday in answer to a judgment summons. Mrs. Fitzgerald stinted that her son could not afford to pay, as he had to keep her. She was the mother of 27 children-21 sons and six daughters.—The Judge : Your son is let off. You deserve cell of your country.

div.head: SOME NEW CHRISTMAS TOTS.
div.p: SOME NEW CHRISTMAS TOTS.

Some very ingenious toys are on sale this year, those of the• mechanical order being very predominant and very novel. Among the expensive things is a perfect model of the Decapod, the huge tank engine built by the Great Eastern Railway this year to cope with suburban traffic. The child of an energetic disposition will enjoy himself in a motor car, big enough for him to ride in. It is propelled •by pedals like a bicycle horse., There is the diver, a little man arrayed in complete uniform, who takes his plunge, remains below for a while, and then returns to the surface like his human counterpart. The clockwork " airship" is having a very large sale. It is suspended, from the ceiling by a string, and, on being wound up, sails round and round in a most realistic fas;iion. A remarkable piece of mechanism is a clock- work train which climbs and descends inclines by means of a cogwheel underneath. This cogwheel only comes into, action when on an inclined track, *here it encounters a rack- rail. The latest train 'novelty is called the " railway smash." This wonderful toy con- sists of two carriages and a goods van, so constructed that when the train is in motion an accident occurs, and the train smashes up in quite a realistic fashion. Of course it can be put together again. Another novelty of the year arc the electric tramcars. They meet each other on a §ingle line, with an occa- sional double track for passing. - The first tram to arrive on the double portion of the line comes automatically to a standstill until the .other has passed the points safely, and then .glides away again.
re-entry into political life is warmly wel- omed on every hand, and Brighton is to b. congratulated.
A VICTORY OF PEACE.

Quite a romance of the war —or rather the peace after the war—is the engagement of General Ben Viljoen to Miss May Belfort, the well known music-hall singer. He is one of the bravest and most popular of our late opponents; and in England lie has always been very well received both in his public and private capacity. Throughout the war he was noted for his gallant and Sporting way of fighting: and the British public is very quick to recognise these qnalities in foe as well as friend. Hence General Viljoen's popularity. Miss May Belfort he met some years ago in London, but it was only a casual acquaintanceship. However, Miss Belfort followed his career during the war

GEN. B. VILJOEN. (4SS MAY BELFORI. with no small interest. After some hair- breadth escapes, he was taken prisoner and sent to St. Helena. Then after the war he came to London to lecture; and again he met his future wife, whom he taught to sing in " taal." She then excepted an en- gagement in Johannesburg: and he went out on the ship; and Miss Belfort ascribes the matrimonial engagement to the long voyage! In the capital of the late republic she made an enormous success with her " taal " singing. She is now singing at the .Palace in London hut ,General Viljoen is in the States, arranc,*- dug the great Boer Exhibit for the St. Louis Exposition.

div.head: " HUMPTY DUMPTY " AT DRURY LANE.
div.p: " HUMPTY DUMPTY " AT DRURY LANE.

This year Drury Lane is to -have the only actual pantomime in the centre of London, though in the suburbs there will be .a score more. In the West End -there will .be instead several Christmas plays, such as "The Cricket on the Hearth," which is already running at the Garrick, - " The Cherry Girl" at the Vaudeville, in which Mr. and Mrs. Seymour Hicks will appear. At Drury Lane the pantomime, which is to be called " Humpty Dumpty," will be the same Brobdingnagian business Mr. Arthur Collins provides every year for the young and the old too. The cast will be even better than usual; and the re- appearance of Mr: , Dan Leno after his sad illness will be particularly popular. He will, of course, only have a very light part, as he is not yet strong enough to bear the brunt of the whole long pantomime twice a day. It is feared that if he did so, he might again .'break down under the awful strain. Mr.

MR. DAN LENO. MR. HERBERT CAMPBELL. Herbert Campbell will as usual appear with him and' is sure to make the fun fast and furious. Mr. Harry Randall has been specially called in to relieve Dan Leno ; and no more popular selection could have been made. The part written in. for him is that of " Little Mary, Minister of the Interior " ! Of the ladies the principal girl is to be Miss Marie George, who made such an enormous hit last year in her Dutch part. So great was it that she has found immediate promotion to. the top of the tree. She is American ; and so is the new principal boy, Miss Louise Willis, who is a fine and very lovely woman. Hitherto she has only been seen in light comedy and comic opera. She has a high soprano voice that made a great hit in " Erminie." Her debut in pantomime will be watched with great interest. The pantomime itself promises to be even better than usual, which is Saving a great deal at Drury Lane.

div.head: SIR E. CLARKE'S NEW ROLE.
div.p: SIR E. CLARKE'S NEW ROLE.

One of the most notable • events in politics is the re-entry of •Sir 'Edward Clarke into the arena. He has been - adopted Conservative candidate for Brighton, and recently made a very interesting and important speech on the all-absorbing fiscal 'question. He ,is a very old. Parliament- ary hand, and held office as Solicitor - Gene- ral, Under the late Marquess of Salisbury for many years. He first entered Parliament in 1880 as member lor Southwark, but was de- f eat eel at a second election in the same year. Fighting- yet a third elec- tion in that same year, he was returned member for Plymouth, and
retained his

scat for that ,constituencv for twenty .ye.:rs without a break. However, in 1900 h,:-; split with them on the question of the rights and the wrongs ,of the Boer war, on which he held extreme Niews. As a result, he resigned his seat and retired into private life, so far as polit•cs -welt; concerned, throwing up his seniority for legal promotion on account of hicprincipit s, and niaking everyone, even •Ws stron ge it opponents, respect him. Sir Edward Clarke is now the leading figure at the Bar, and almost the last of a pa act' any brilliant circle .of barristers who ac now either dead or on the b. rich, and he has himself been frequently mentioned for the Woolsack. The son of a City jeweller, he was called to the Bar just on forty years ago, and gradually worked his way to the front. The Penge case and the " Turf Frauds Detectives" case finally set their seal ,on his reputation, and since then he has been briefed in practically every important trial.

div.head: WOMAN WHO SAVED THE QUEEN.
div.p: THE WOMAN WHO SAVED THE QUEEN.

That her Majesty owes her life to the Hon. Miss Charlotte Knollys' prompt warning when the fire broke out at Sandringham last week was not fully realised by the public for the moment, but there is now no doubt that had this lady been a few moments longer in waking her Majesty a very serious, if not fatal, acci- - dent would have happened to our Queen. Miss Knollys awoke at about five % a.m. almost choked. The room was full of dense wreaths of blinding smoke. Tongues of flame were - already• curling round the wood- (i) work over the door and crack- ing the plaster in the ceiling. The Queen was
not .warned a TH moment too
soon, for almost

immediately on her leaving the room the ceil- ing fell in. The house brigade proved efficient, and from the hydrant on the terrace, just underneath the Queen's bedroom, was soon pouring through the smoke-shrouded w;n'ilows a steady stream of water. In about twenty minutes the flames were extinguished. It appears that the heat from the lire in Miss linollys' room, penetrating the concrete, had set the underlying beam smouldering, and in all probability the Tar]; had been eating- its way into the wood for several days efore it finally sprang into flame. The bla2e then began to creep along until it burst through the ceiling of her Majesty's room right over the door.

div.head: DISCOVEEY FIASCO.
div.p: THE DISCOVEEY FIASCO.

As the time of year is 'coming round when the ice barrier round the South Polar regions opens to the outer world for a short time, the Terra Nova has sailed urder Admiralty orders from Tasmania for Macmurdo Bay in search of the Discovery, which lies there in latitude 77.49 S embedded in the ice. Captain Scott and his brave men have been locked in with- out communication with the outer world for close on a- year, and things are in a very satisfactory state. The Terra Nova is taking all, possible comforts out to the Discovery, and a very large mail for the whole crew. One letter of peculiar interest is that of Sir Clements Markham, the President of the Royal

div.head: fERRA
div.p: fERRA

eographical Society, to Captain Scott, Which, though most kindly and tactfully worded, will be a gre; t blow to the brave captain. It is simply nothing more or less than an intimation that the funds available have practically come to an end. With the strictest economy they can be made to last out till next October; but it practically means the immediate return of the expedition. Other questions raised as to tho quality of the food, etc., are all to stand over in view of the principal one. The Govern- ment are bearing the costs of the relief exp.- dition, and have taken over the Morning pet - contra. It Is a great pity that the expedi- tion should have ended in a financial fiasco, and it will be a great blow to Captain Scott.

div.head: SALFORD v. HULL.
div.p: SALFORD v. HULL.

Played at Weaste, in tine, but gloomy weather, before 4000 people. Salford started, and after Moxon had missed a good opportunity for the visitors, Lomas for Salford kicked three penalty goals. in the second half, the home side were mainly the aggressors, and Taylor saved repeatedly. Norris scored far Sal- ford, Lomas landing a goal. Result—Salford, 4 goals 1 try (11 points); Hull, nil. HELL KINGSTON ROVERS v. SWINTON.

At Hull, before 3,000 spetators. The Rovers kicked off, and invaded Swinton's territory. Gay dropped a goal from a scrimmage. There was no further score to half-time. On the restart, the Rovers were rather pressed, and twice Swinton came near scoring, but each time failed to cross the line. The game was rough most all through; the referee remonstrating with two or three Swinton players. Result—Rovers, 1 dropped goal; Swinton, niL

div.head: WIGAN v. BATLEY
div.p: WIGAN v. BATLEY

At Central Park, Wigan, before a capital attendance. Hilton started, and Batley had a short spell on the attack. Eventually Sbarrock scored fr Wigan, but no goal was kicked. On resuming, Wigan scored again through Harris and Leythain. Result—Wigan, 14 points; Batley, nil.
BRADFORD v. KEIGHLEV.

At Bradford, in thick fog. In the first half, Keighley pressed at the opening. Then Dunbavin scored, and later Myers dropped a goal, the teams changing ends with a point between them. On resuming, Sinton scored, and Gunn kicked a goal. Play could not now be followed, but, so far as could be judged, was in Bradford's favour. Result—Bradford, I.goal 2 tries (8 points); Keighley, 1 g,,..1 (2 points).

div.head: FRIENDLY MATCH.
div.p: FRIENDLY MATCH.
WARRINGTON " A " v. WIDNES RANG ER S..

Warrington "A " • had a ridiculously easy task on Saturday, when Widnes Rangers visited the Wilderspool enclosure and retired vanquished to the tune of 41 points to nil. From the outset the home team had matters all their own way, and Short soon got over. The try was not improved upon. Kenyon was in splendid form, and allowed no opportunities to slip. Before the interval he had scored four tries, after capital runs, converted one ; and kicked a penalty goal. Forster added the extra points in one case. At half- time the score read :—Warrington, 21 points; Widnes Rangers, nil. On resuming, the Warrington men speedily improved their lead, and the Widnesians never had a look in. Kenyon placed three tries to his credit and the other scorers were Mahoney, Short, and Foster. Final :—Warrington, four goals, eleven tries (41 points) .; Widnes Rangers, nil.

div.head: INTER-WORKS LEAGUE.
div.p: INTER-WORKS LEAGUE.
CROSFIELD'S V. LONDON AND NORTH-WESTERN RAILWAY.

The above teams met on Crosfield's ground, on Satur- day, neither side being at full strength. The North- Western soon got to work as the game was but a iew moments old when Lloyd gave Jackson a change, and the latter, after a splendid dodgy run grounded in good position. The railway continued to hold the upper hand, the backs especially being in rare form, and from d sequence of transfers Timmins scored try number two. Lloyd added another all on his own, whilst Jackson piled on the agony by recording his second try after a dashing run, Taylor in one instance added the extra points. Half-time L. & N.-W, 1 goal 4 tries, Crosfield's nil. After the change of ends, the play was all in favour of the visitors, the homesters constantly defending. The Loco's again &ot going and a smart passing bout saw Jackson crossing at the corner, no goal resulting. After several minutes play the•,game was brought to an abrupt termination owing to a painful mishap to one of Crosfield's men and the game ended. L. & N.-W. R. 1 goal 5 tries (17 points), Crosfield's nil.

div.head: NORTHERN UNION.
div.p: THE NORTHERN UNION.
SIRST DIVISION.
LEEDS v. WARRINGTON

About 5,000 spectators braved the foggy and unpleas- ant conditions on Saturlay to see the first League fixture between these teams at Headingley. Detailed description of the play is impossible for the reason that it was only during the last ten minutes that what was happening on one( touch line could be seen from the other.

Grace's kick-off was followed by a rush of the home forwards to the Warrington line, where Hallam was found, and continued throughout the game, in fine defensive mood. Both sides attacked in turn after this, but without scoring advantage. Then Birch and Hewlett began a dribble which established play in the Warrington " 25." From the next scrummage Grace and Mosley got the ball among the three-quarters, and Evans raced away for the line. In a tackle by Fish and one of the forwards the old Parish Church wing man was injured and had to retire for the rest of the first half. A fine bid fora score by Llewellyn and Tay- lor was just spoiled by Hallam; and then Isherwood, with a brilliant individual effort, raised the siege and took play to the Leeds end, half-time arriving with nothing scored. Leeds were at full strength in the second half, Evans rejoining his colleagues. rho result was that the Lan- cashire forwards were now badly beaten in the scrum- mages, and their half backs only rarely got the ball. Individual players could not be identified in the thick fog, and at one point it seemed certain that the game would have to be stopped. Fortunately the air cleared considerably in the last few minutes, and the spectatm:s weie able to see the Leeds backs execute a fine passing movement, which ended in Llewellyn scoring a try— the only point the match yielded. Result :—Leeds, 1 try (3 points) ; Warrington, nil. Teams : Leeds—H. Littlewood, back; W. Evans, J. P. Jenkins, T. Llewellyn and T. W. Davies, three-quarter backs; G. Grace and G. E. Mosley, half backs; J. G. Moffat, G. Hewlett, J. W. Stead, J. W. Birch, F. Webster, T. Taylor, E. Barrett, and W. Woolf, forwards. Warrington—Hallam, back; Fish, Isherwood, Dicken- son and Hockenhall, three-quarter backs; Davies and Bate, half backs; Morrison, Boardman, Swift, Thomas, Cook, Lunt, Jolley, and Naylor, forwards. Referee, Mr. J. Bruckshaw (Stockport). Touch judges, Mr. H. Farrar (tieighley) and Mr. R. L. Smith (Bradford).

RUNCORN v. LEIGH. Played at Runcorn, before a small attendance. Panne started, and play for a time was evenly contested. Run-r corn then attacked, and from a fine round of passing in which Jolley, Price, Butterworth and Jones took part, the last named scored. Farmer added a goal. Resum- ing, Leigh transferred play to the Runcorn end. where Burgess dropped a goal. Pearson put in some good defensive work-,and Runcorn were gradually forced back again. Burgesl sent the ball over the Runcorn line, Hough touching dead just in time. Tomlinson retired hurt, but resumed play. _ Just before the interval _
RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

div.head: Intemperance and Pauperism.
div.p: Intemperance and Pauperism.

Mr. J. Stokes presided over the monthly meeting of the Runcorn Board of Guardians which was held at Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday afternoon. There were also present :—Messrs. A. R. Norman (vice-chairman), S. Woodward. T. Wright, S. Taylor, A. G. Guest, H. Mawdsley, J. Mounfield, G. Piling, T. Clarke, C. Roy- lance, E. Bretherton, J. L. Jones, E. Lewis, J. Mclntyre, T. Wood, J. Edwards, J. Douglas, A. H. Talbot, J. Whitlow, T. Lewis, R. Billington, J. Spruce, G. F. A3hton (clerk), W. E. Hough (assistant), T. Cook, T. Riley, and W. De Prez (relieving officers), and. W. Cunnah (headmaster).

THE MAINTENANCE OF PAUPER LUNATICS. At the interim meeting of the Board the Guardians considered a communication from the Birkenhead Union suggesting that a joint committee should be formed to manage the two county asylums at Upton and Parkside, with a view to fixing a uniform charge for the mainten- ance of pauper lunatics. The Board were of the opinion that the proposal if adopted would increase the expense and therefore could not see their way to support it. The Clerk said he had now received a further letter stating that the Birkenhead Union made the request to the County Council but the authority _,,decided that they could not make any alteration.

div.head: UNEMPLOYED.
div.p: THE UNEMPLOYED.

The Lambeth (f.:Onao-n) Board of Guardians wrote stating that they had recently under consideration the question of means to be adopted to procure work for the unemployed and thereby prevent them and their wives and families from becoming a burden on the rates. Although the question was one which might be considered not to affect Boards of Guardians until an application for relief be actually made, yet the means of avoiding the necessity for such application should in the opinion of that Board receive the careful attention of all poor law authorities. The limited powers which Boards of Guardians possessed were in most instances of little or no avail in dealing with this important subject. Locally it appeared to the Guardians that all that could be done was to appeal to the Borough and County Councils to undertake during the !present winter such necessary work as would insure the employ- ment o 6 the maximum amount of labour it was possible to engage. The problem was in the opinion of the Board one which ought not to be left to local authorities but,should be dealt with by the Government. The undertaking of national works on a large scale and of a remunerative description would give employment to many who would otherwise be forced to seek relief from the parish. The support of the Board was asked for.

The Chairman said ha could scarcely remember having seen so many unemployed in Runcorn as there appeared to be at present. The prospect was very serious if the winter should happen to be a severe one.
The matter wa.s.refer-re-dt-O the.Pa-rli-r;menLlry Corn- mittee.

INTEMPERANCE AND PAUPERISM. The Haslingdon Union forwarded copies of the following resolutions having reference to the reduction of licences and the conttol of clubs where intoxicating liquors are sold : "That this Board of Guardians desires to place on record the fact that the accommoda- tion of the House is taxed to its utmost capacity by reason of the great increase in the number of children under the care of the Board and the Board regrets to find that in the great majority of cases children get here in consequence of the intemperance of one or both parents, and that in view of these facts the Board desires to urge upon the licensing .magistrates throughout the Union the desirability of carefully considering the necessities of each neighbourhood, and of exercising to the utmost their powers in the interest not only of the ratepayers but of the poor children who are sent here in ',conse- quence of the innumerable temptations to drink which cause their parents to transgress the law, and so cruelly neglect their children," and that tteopy of the resolu- tion be forwarded to the members for the Rossendale and Accrington Divisions, the Prime Minister, Home Secretary and all Boards of Guardians,with the observa- tion that in our opinion more drastic legislation is desirable than now exists to diminish or put down the drinking in clubs." Mr. Jones moved that the letter lie on the table. Mr. Wright seconded, remarking that he thought the resolutions were a reflection on the magistrates who, at the present time, were doing their utmost to prevent an increase in licences where it was not required. Mr. Norman: I don't agree with that.. T think the idea is to strengthen aye hands of the magistrates. (Hear, hear...)
Mr. Wood inoposed that the Board shnuld support the resolutions. "

Mr. Douglqs seconded. Mr. Pilling moved that the matter be referred to the Parliamentary Committee but there was no seconder. On a vote baing taken it was decided by a majority of 13 tO5 to support the resolutions.

THE RATIWO-M AND LAVATORY ACCOMMODATION. The Local Government Board wrote approving the plan of the proposed new bathroom and lavatory at the Runcorn Workhouse. An expenditure not exceeding £256 was sanctioned.
It was decided to advertise for tenders for the carry- ing out of the work.
THE INCREASE IN VAGRANCY.

The Guardians of the Caistor Union forsVarded a copy of the following resolution, with a request that the Runcorn Guardians should pass a similar one That this Board of Guardians call the attention of his Majesty's Gevernment to the alarming increase in the number of vagrants and to urge that this question be -dealt with by the establishment of labour colonies or otherwise.",

The Guardians of Heinsworth Union forwarded a copy of the following resolution. If the Runcorn Board were of the same opinion they were requested to communicate with His Majesty's Prison Commission- ers in the matter :—" That this Board having had its attention drawn to the report of His Majesty's Com- missioners of-prisons for 190-3, is of opinion that the remarks contained therein regarding the treatment of vagrants in tramp wards are entirely uncalled for. They are further of opinioß that the efforts made by Boards of Guardians to deal satisfactorily with the pro- fessional vagrant in many cases at great expense to the ratepayers, will always be rendered nugatory so long as the excessively lenient treatment of refractory tramps in gaol causes them to look upon the prison as a refuge and comfortable temporary home." The letters were referred to the Parliamentary Com- mittee.

div.head: EDUCATION SUII-COMMITTEE.
div.p: THE EDUCATION SUII-COMMITTEE.
. -- Mr. Pilling moved that the Education Sub-committee be allowed the use of the board room for their meet- ings. He pointed out that up to the present the coin-
mittee had been meeting in the Court House, Frodsham, which was inconvenient and unsuitable.
Mr. Woodward seconded the proposition which was agreed to.
FINANC I At.

Mr. Woodward reported that there was a balance in the hands of the treasurer of £2,809 17s. 9d. He called attention to the fact that the following townships had not paid the calls dne on November 13th :—Acbon Grange, Alvanley, Budworth, Grappenhall, Kekewick, Kingsley, Moore, Seven Oaks and Sutton. He moved that the clerk be instructed to apply for immediate payment. This was carried.

Mr. Roylance said that at Moore they were waiting for the new valuation list to be prepared by the Assess- ment Committee. Mr. Woodward said that was no excuse as the assistant overseer had not, he believed, been told to defer col- lecting the rate.
THE WORKHOUSE.-LARGE NUMBER OF VIGRANTS.

Mr. Wood reported that the House Committee had de- cided for the presentithat all leave of absence and visiting of inmates should be discontinued owing to the preval- ence of smallpox in the Warrington Union. The number of inmates of the house—which showed a great decrease —was 143. During the month 170 vagrants had passed through the house as compared with 114 for the corres- ponding period last year. The Chairman: That quite justifies the letters we have received from other Boards on the subject of vagrancy. Mr. Jones: It is on account of bad trade. Wait until we get the new fiscal policy. (Laughter.) The minutes were confirmed.

div.head: PURIFY THE BLOOD.
div.p: PURIFY THE BLOOD.

Good health is impossible without pure blood. Every organ of the body is kept in perfect order by the blood that courses through our veins. How important it is then, that it should be pure and undefiled. Otherwise, each organ that it passes through becomes contamin- ated with disease. A breakdown is found to occur. Then from unsightly pimples, blotches, and such like outward signs of Impure Blood, greater evils spring. Indigestion, constipation kidney disease, and a host of others all have their foundation in the blood. "Poor- ness of blood had for many years been a constant source- of trouble tb me." With the taking of Dr. Morse's .Indian Root Pills, a large sore that would never heal has quite vanished. They have also toned up my blood to a remarkable degree. div.head: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.
div.p: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.
Emmanuel Church.

On Sunday sermons were preached at Emmanuel Church, Bold-street, by the Bev. F. Vaughan. At each service there was a fairly large congregation, the offor tories being on behalf of the church expenses.

div.head: Latchford Primitive Methodist Church.
div.p: Latchford Primitive Methodist Church.

A "llosan-nah Service" was held at this church ea Sunday afternoon. The Legh-street choir, under the conductorship af Mr. A. Spruce, rendered "Gloria." (12th Mass) and "0 worship the King," with good taste. Miss Amy Mansell sang Throw ont the life-line." Several recitations were contributed. The Rev. J. Garlham Reed presided, and gave an address. Pastor Grady also assisted. Mr. Fred Podmore presided at the

Legh Street Primitive Methodist Church. At this place of worship on Sunday the pulpit was occupied in the morning by Mr. S. Albinson. The Rev. J. Gardham Reed preached in the evening on the sub- ject "Every man's life a special plan of God." The organ voluntaries for the day were :—" Largo" (Rink), "Triumphal March" (Lemmens), Adagio-2nd Organ Sonata (Mendelssohn), "But the Lord is mindful" belpg contributed by the organist, Mr. Fred Podmore. Mr. Barnes, baritone, sang "The Gentle Shepherd" at the evening service.

St. Peter's Christmas Open Sunday. An open secvice in connection with the Meu'g Bible Class was held at St. Peter's Church on Sunday and was largely attended. Mr. T. S. Steel presided, and the service was conducted by the Rev. D. B. James. The Firth Glee party, under the conductorship of Mr. Edward Roberts, sang "In Absence,"" The Little Church." and' Lead, kindly Light," in a very effective and pleasing manner. An address was given by the Rev. C. J. Edwards, curate of St. Paul's, who took for his subject " What think ye of Christ ?- The collec- tion. which amounted to a very satisfactory sum, was in aid of church expenses. Wycliffe P S.A. Society.

At, the P.S.A. meeting held on Sunday last, at 'which there was an average] attendance, Mr. W. H. J. Jenkins took the chair and spoke upon the better side of men's lives. They should always try, he said. tro see the good inirach other, and so work together, for the elevation of their fellows. To this end let ;hem try to make thek lives pure, filled with earnestness for the good of all. Mr. A. Bathtrate, of Liverpool, was the speaker. He spoke upon" What we believe." Upon many things, he said our beliefs differed. Our lives were guided by what we believed. Columbus for instance,- believed there was land and neople beyond the seas, and his belief impelled him there. To the pastas in the preseot, great minds had been influenced by their beliefs— Wilberforce for liberty, Gladstone for sympathy with the oppressed, Luther for the Gospel of Christ, Christians- for the brotherhood of man. Belief was not only helpful, but sometimes a great hindrance. As Christ said, "He could not do manv mighty deeds amongst them because of their unbelief.' It mattered much what we believed. There was a difference between the agnostic and the Christian. The former believed in what he could see, but the Christian lived by faith, and believed by faith in the future, and so brought to him- self happiness now, visions of brightness for the future, and the eternal home prepared for the faithful-believing , children of Go.—The Secretary announced that a, new I member had joined them, making the total 54S.—Mr. Owen and Mr, A. Healey took part in the meeting.—Mr. Payton presided at the organ. •

The Public Health. The Registrar-General reports that the animal -rate of mortality in the seventy-six great towns of England and Wales last week averaged 19.2 per 1,000. The rate in Liverpool was 24, Birkenhead 22, Wallasey 14, Bootle' 20, St. Helens 24, Wigan 30, Warrington 17, Preston 22, and Barrow-in-Furness 13. Grimsby's 6 was the lowest rate, and Merthyr Tydvil's 32 the highest.
PUBLIC BENEFIT. UNDER the CLOCK for BES BOOTS in LANCASHIRK.—Advt. The Corporation Gas Works. - -

The annual inspection of the gas works by the mem- bers of the 0-as Committee took place' yesterday and the general opinion was expressed that the Works are in a very satisfactory condition. Subsequently at the invitation of the Chairman of the committee (Alder- man James Fairclough) the members lunched at the Town Hall. All the members 'were present, together with some of the chief officials. It will be remem- bered that the committee has this year handed over in relief of the rates £B,OOO, and has also reduced the price of gas by one penny per thousand feet. It is anticipated that next year's results will be equally good.

The members Of this society spent pleasant social evening together on Monday evening. At the outset the members were invited to answer a number of questions, conundrums and acrostics which were dis- played round the room. Some of the answers which were written proved highly amusing. The casket scene in Shakespeare's "Merchant of Venice"• was represented and proved an acceptable item in the programme. Light refreshments were partaken of. In the second half Mr. Hibbert contributed a song, and Mr. William Brown and Mr. James Gould proved themselves capable entertainers.

The Smallpox Epidemic.—A Foolish Prejudice There have been several fresh cases of smallpox during the past week. Unfortunately one woman has died of the disease without being medically attended to. She seems to have objected to a doctor being .- brought in, probably from a fear of being removed to the hospital. The result has been that many neighbours have visited her and probably contracted the disease. On hearing of the case, the health officials took prompt measures for the burial of the deceased woman and the isolation of those who had been in close contact with her. There are grave fears that other cases may arise from this one, but the authorities are doing all that is possible to prevent the spread of the disease, and the latest reports are that their precautionary measures promise to be suc- cessful.—An official of the Local Government Board has visited the town this week, and conferred with the authorities on the measures being taken to stay the progress of the disease in the:town. Local Church Conference. A conference of the clergy and lay representatives of ,the Rural Deanery of Winwiek was held at the Assembly Rooms, Bridge-street (over Toft's Shop), Warrington on Thursday afternoon. The Rev. Canon Penrhyn, Rural Dean, presided and there was a re- presentative attendance. The Rev. E. C. E. Carleton was re-elected secretary and Mr. E. Draper was invited to undertake the duties of treasurer. The following representatives were appointed on diocesan committees: Finance Association, Rev. Canon Willis. Smith, Captain Withington ; Standing Committee of Diocesan Conference, Rev. Morley Stevenson, Mr. J. D. Buckton Mr. R. Stone ; Board of Education, Rev. J. Davies, Mr. J. D. Buckton; Church Aid Society, Rev. Canon Penrhyn,Dr. Mouncey. A discussion ensued with reference to the Liverpool Cathedral scheme. It was suggested that a secretary be appointed in each parish to endeavour to raise subscriptions. Eight clergymen and sixteen laymen were appointed on the general committee of the Church Congress .which will meet in Li;verpool early in October next. It was suggested by the Rev. Canon Willis that the Ruri-Decanal, conferences be held more frequently and the suggestion met with general approval. Warrington Wesleyan Methodist Circuit.
