div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
DRIDIZIBER 19th 1903.
MR. CHAMBERLAIN THE CHAMPION abounds in surprises ADVERTISER. and if his Leeds

speeches contained for the most part a re-hash of stale fallacies there was a new spice in the "resurrection pie." There is to be a Caamberlain Commission of inquiry into the:Fiscg.l question. A Royal Commission has been scouted by his supporters as a mere pretext for delay. Unmeasured scorn has been heaped upon everybody who suggested this method of taking the evidence. But Mr. CHAMBERLAIN'S CODA- M:SSIOri will have a more than Royal authority, and it will als have the electioneer- ing advantage of keeping his views steadily before the public. At Leeds he showed consider- able impatience with Ma. Asourrtr,who persists in cross-examining him as if he were a witness on oath. But this method will be perfectly correct when it is practised by Mn. CHAMBERLAIN'S Com- mission. The Free Trade witnesses, if they are willing to testify, will be cross-examined by the Birmingham counsel for Protection. As an entertainment this might have its occasional merits; but is the country going to take it as a serious investigation? Here is a one-sided tribunal which is simply a Committee of the Tariff Reform League,and MR.CHAMBERLAIN gravely asks us to believe that it;is competent to frame a tariff which will save a great deal of time and labour when Mr. AUSTEN CHA3IBERLAIN is preparing his first Protectionist Budget! Of course there is nothing r,o hinder the Tariff Reform League from indulging in this fantasy. Mr. CHAMBERLAIN may collect a number of manufacturers,who will arrange a tariff to suit what they suppose to be the interests of their respective trades. He may even find experts to speak for the Colonies and for India But when the comedy is played, who will attach to it any more weight than belongs to Mr. VirrcE's leaflets? Why should experts who do not agree with Mr.• CHAMBERLAIN appear before his Com- mission? It is a nice little game, but he cannot expect his opponents to play it. This new device for keeping the pot boiling is supplemented by the suggestion that Mr. CHAMBERLAIN Should repair in person to the Colonies to persuade them to a bargain. "Let them send me." Is this a mandate to the Cabinet which exists solely for the purpose of fulfilling Mr. CHAMBERLAIN'S behests? With the Birmingham Commission modelling a tariff day by day, and with Mr. CHAMBERLAIN " Stumping " the Colonies, there would not be much use for a Ministerial programme. We my be sure that Mr. CHAMBER- LAIN would not be closeted with the Colonial states- men all the while in secret conference. He would enlighten the public mind in Australia with flashes of his humorous economics. We should have long reports of him in the " Times," as we had when he was in South Africa. Thus he would continue to eclipse the Cabinet, and Mr. BALFOUR would have great difficulty in getting his party to pay any attention to War Office reform, and what not. But this would not matter if the time were pleasantly filled up by Mr. CHAMBERLAIN and his experts until the party oaganisation fixed the moment for a dissolu- tion. For all these tactics are conducted with an eye to this eventuality. It is not to be imagined that when Parliament meets, and the Government make a show of getting to work upon legislation, Mr. CHAMBERLAIN,wiII sub- side into the attitude of a spectator. He does not care a button about the 'Government legisla- tion. He will be eager to invent some new ad- vertisement for his patent medicine. The "Times" has lately employed every conceivable form of entreaty to the public to buy a certain book. We have been greeted daily with feverish warnings not to miss our last chance. Mr. CHAMBERLAIN is pursuing the same method with his panacea for the Empire. "Take my Model Tariff and save the Empire for your sons, Reject this Un- exampled Offer and Rush co Ruin! Only a Few Weeks More, and there may be a Dissolution. Britons, Awake ! " Mr. CHAMBERLAIN is a Champion advertiser, but the country does not want the goods.
THE party organisa- TETE LONDON tion of the Unionists ELECTIONS. is still pretty sound

in the London con— stituencies. 'net is the one clear moral to be drawn from Dalwich and L ovisharn. The not un- natural surprise of the Ministerialists at their success makes their rapture a little extravagant. The " Times " had ostentatiously prepared for .defeat, or at least for a narrow escape, and it is rather at. a loss for judicious phrases to express its joy. Mr.CHAMBERLAIN'S policy,we are told,if not triumphantly vindicated, is supported by "strik- ing negative evidence." The striking negative is really given to the hasty assumption that London would exhibit in a marked way the disintegratio n of the Unionists that is going on throughout the country. "Typical middle-class metropolitan coo - stituencies," says the" Standard," "remain firmly attached to the Unionist Cause." For Dulwich and Lewisham the Unionist cause is still some- thing to cling to, in spite of the confusion of new issues. There, at all events, it seems probable that the DUKE OF DEVONSHIRE'S attitude is no t understood. If the Dulwich and Lewisham Unionists were to rem&n firmly attached to the Unionist cause, they did not see how they were to take the DUKE'S advice, and either vote ag %lust the Ministerial candidates or stay away from the poll. The DUKE, from the Unionist party man'

gap.desc: skipped/gap: fewer than 20 non-control characters after cleanup

div.head: Examiner, Saturday December 19, 1903
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday December 19, 1903

point of view, is in a somewhat anomalous posi- tion. It may be presumed that he is stilt firmly attached to the Unionist cause, and yet the evidence on the subject may have appeared to many electors as rather like a "striking negative." He endeavoured, at any rate, to distinguish between gripport for Mr. CHAMBERLAIN and sup- port for Mr. BALFOUR ; and as this is a distinction without a difference his council to Unionist voters has fallen rather flat. Perhaps this will help him towards the conclusion that it is now impossible to remain firmly attached to the Unionist cause, whatever that may be, and at the same time to champion the much more pressing cause of Free Trade. The old issue must d'sappear, and the dividing line of parties mast be the line between Free Traders and Protectionists. For all practical purposes there is no such thing as a Unionist party. Every man who voted for Dr. RUTHER- FOORD HARRIS and Major COATES voted for Protec- tion.

This simple truth is still hidden from eyes that do not want to see it. "Unionists of all shades," says the " Standard," " must, at any rate, feel gratified by this proof of the tenacity with which their doctrines are held in the mercantile and trad- ing sections of London society." !Manifestly these doctrines, whatever they are, can be of little coh- sequence when men who hold them vote for the Fiscal policy of Mr. BALFOUR and Mr. CHAMBER- LAIN. The " Standard " endeavours to comfort itself with the reflection that Dr. HARRIS and Major 00.A.TES did not pledge themselves to every jot and tittle of Mr. CHAMBERLAIN'S :proposals. "We trust that Mr. CHAMBERLAIN will recognise the true meaning of this attitude on the part of- those who sympathise with his efforts, and that he will abandon a project which is obviously considered unsuitable to bring forward at a contested election." Of all the con elusions to be drawn from Dulwich and Lewisham this is certainly the most original. Major °OATES and Dr. HARRIS have been returned as supporters of the BALFOUR-CHAMBERLAIN compact in two typically Conservative constituencies ; and it needs a singular imagination to behold in this result a discouragement for Mr. CHAMBERLAIN. There are people, no doubt, who still distinguish between his proposals and Mr. BALFOUR'S. Mr. RIDER HAGGARD writes to the " Times " that " the latter must work the utter ruin of the land and husbandry of Britain." For this reason Mr. HAGGARD and his agricultural friends in the Central Chamber are" supporters of the policy which at least does not propose to leave land- owners, farmers, and labourers to perish, starved and frozen in the Free Trade frost, while, !through its windows, they watch the business and city folk full fed and warmed at the Protection fire in the Imperial house to he built by MR. CHAMBER- LAIN." The notion that MR. BALFOUR'S policy would leave MR. HAGGARD in the mournful sit- uation he describes in such imaginative prose is not warranted by the political situation. He harrows the feelings of his friends without cause. MR. BALFOUR is really quite at one with MR. HAGGARD in the belief that a two shilling duty will enable the farmer to warm both hands at the Protection fire. But whatever promise of this cheering blaze they may see in Dulwich and Lewisham will be extinguished by the General Election.

Ratepayers who are feeling the burden of the Education rate will hear with satisfaction that the Government intend in the ensuing session of Parliament to bring in a Bill to relieve local rates from all charges connected with education and make the whole cost an imperial charge. By this step the Government hope to kill the passive resistance movement. Judging by the parlous condition of the Government and taking into con- sicieration the drastic nature of this suggested change in the form of educational maintenance the passing of the measure is a somewhat remote possibility. However, the scheme itself indicates a gratifying tendency in high quarters towards a thoroughly nationalised scheme of education.

Elec%ions, both Parliamentary and municipal, are usually followed by free allegations of bribery and corruption. Warrington has indulged in a plethora of elections lately, and there has been a proportionate—or disproportionate—number of charges against candidates and their workers of using illegal means to influence the electors. The town is either a second Shrewsbury or a large num- ber of people are "strangers to the truth" as Oouncillor Lord would say. Yesterday, one of the newly-elected repres3nuatives of Bewsey Ward, Councillor Gough, was summoned to the Borough Police Court to answer a charge of bribery,but the case was adjourned until Wednesday next. The pro- ceedings have, naturally enough, caused a local sensation, for no such charge has ever before been preferred in the Borough Police Court. Oa this p trticular ;Aso we are, of course, unable to offer any comment while it is sub iudiee. If Dame Rumour is to be believed, however, similar pro- eeedings should be taken against more than one Councillor, and various publicans are alleged to be trembling in their shoes 'act " treating " should be too closely inquire:l into. There is another oppor- tunity here for the " purity party" to be up and doing, and we doubt not that the leader,Councillor Dodds, will show no hesitation in condemning any corrupt electioneering that may be exposed.

The Warrington Savings Bank was established so far back as 1818, bat this venerable institution does not show the E. lightest signs of decay or ill- access. Oa the contrary it grows from strength to strength. A comparative statement of the business of the institution for the last twenty-two years shows that the total number of transactions has increased from 13.972 in 1882 to 28,268 last year,and the amount now standing to the credit of depositors is £355,192 or I:80,000 more than twenty-two years ago. Even such a pessimist on our present position as Mr. Chamberlain cannot convince us that things are going badly with the Savings Bank. The institution has a record of uninterrupted progress and its success must in some measure reflect the financial position of the large number of depositors who make use of it. When it is considered that the gteater proportion of the transactions are of saiali amounts, and that there are 5,880 depositors, whose accounts do not exceed one pound, it win be seen that some of the very poorest in the town are able to provide to a small extent against a "rainy day." Unfortun- ately there are many, who will not, although they have the opportunity, provide for old age and creeping infirmities, and these people generally spend the evening of their days in the Workhouse or live on the charity of their more thrifty friends and relatives.

Successful as was the last Warrington Show in many respects, the statement of alcounts which was presented to the members of the Agricultural Society on Wednesday was hardly satisfactory. There was a loss of £152. It is probable that the rain which fell during the afternoon of show day interfered somewhat with the attendance, but even if ideal weather had prevailed the admissions at the gate would not havebeen sufficient to make the show pay its way. Fortunately the society has a president who is determined to keep the finances on a sound footing even if he has to make up the yearly deficit out of his own pocket. Last year he gave a special donation of £3OO and this year he has made a further donation of £l5O, with the result that the society is able to carry forward a balance in hand of £65. It woilld, of course, be more satisfactory if the society could meet its liabilities without relying on the generosity of the President, and as it becomes better established probably it may be able to do so. There is much

room for improvement in the number of entries in many of the classes. Warrington is surrounded by one of the richest agricultural tracts in England, and the appeal of the committee for more general support from those interested in the improvement of stock should not fall upon deaf ears.

The lamentable loss of life resulting from un- protected fires in houses called forth strong but justifiable comment from Coroner Brighouse on Monday. It is a matter for serious reflection that so many children should come to an untimely and psinful end through the neglect of parents to pro- vide efficient fireguards. During the past three months it has been Mr. Brighouse's lot to investi- gate no fewer than thirteen burning fatalities in which the victims were young chi;dren. In a num- ber of cases quoted,the circumstances were identi- cal. Children were left alone in rooms where there were unprotected fires and, on returning, their parents were distressed to find that they had sustained fatal burns. Mr. Brighouse seems to despair of ever being able to convince many parents of the folly of such conduct. Legislation, he says,is the only remedy,iand he intends at every similar inquest in his district to ask for an ex- pression of opinion, such as the jury gave vent to on Monday, in favour of an Act of Parliament practically making efficient :fireguards compulsory. A good suggestion which the jury threw out— that builders of cottage property should provide guards—is worthy of careful consideration. One cannot restrain a feeling:of sympathy with the poor to whom every item of expenditure moans an increased difficulty in making ends meet, and if the suggestion were acted upon it would be no mean advance in the right direction.

Writing of SyJney brings to mind the greaf- struggle for "the ashes of English cricket which has been going on there this week. The intense excitement of the Australian crowd has been re- flected ~ver here—or should we say "up here " in an uncommon degree thanks to the perfection of the modern cable and newspaper enterprise. We have had the opportunity, day by day, of see- ing, in the mind's eye, every ball bowled through- out the first test match. Six days' play is some- what of a novelty for a cricket match, and to those actively concerned it must be a severe strain. Old England's representatives have emerged from the ordeal undismayed and covered with glory. To defeat the ;nighty men of Australia by five wickets on their own turf at the first time of asking augurs well for the return of those" ashes." Of course, other English teams have won the first test game—and lost the rest—but somehow we have more confidence in Pelham Warner's much criticised but capable band. Away with any prognostications of failure. Let us instead sing the praises of Foster, " the record extinguisher," of Braund and Hayward and Hirst, who have pulled the thing through in so gallant a style. There has only been one unplea- sant incident, so far, and that was the unsport- manlike, boorish " barracking "of the Melbourne umpire who gave an unpopular decision. It is a matter for thankfulness that the Australian cricketers themselves are thorough sportsmen and strongly discountenance the tend- ency to hooliganism on the part of the crowd. We should hesitate to say that an Australian crowd is devoid of any instinct of fair play and good sportsmanship, but another such outburst as the one at Sydney will disgust the English cricketers and their admirers beyond measure.

English eangfroid is a characteristic of the nation, and one of considerable value. The "Sydney Bulletin" hits off this view of the case very neatly, as follows: "It is greatly due to their cold-blooded indifference that the English race has got on in the world. Englishmen have never been annoyed or bad-tempered when called liars or horse thieves by bilious foreigners. Not a bit! They went on carving another slice of territory off the globe and erecting a few more churches and breweries. Many a bit of territory has Britain got while foreigners were dancing excitedly like cats on hot plates, and explaining hox wrong it was of that country to take the previous bit." The " churches and breweries " point is particularly good.

The financial bearings of Mr. Chamberlain's scheme from the point of view of the working class was admirably put by Mr. W. S. Robson, M.P., in his speech at Bow the other day. Ac- cording to Mr. Ritchie, the taxation specially imposed in order to raise revenue during the war was divided in such proportion that about £18,000,000 was paid by the wealthier class in the form of Income-Tax, while £15,000,000 was paid by the industrial class through the increased duties on sugar and tea and the corn tax. Now the Government has since relieved the Income-Tax payers by removing £10,500,000 of the £18,000,000 placed upon their shoulders by the war, and Mr. Austen Chamberlain, the Chan- cellor of the Exchequer, has promised this class still further remissions. What, however, does Mc. Chamberlain propose P By new duties on wheat and meat he expects 150 raise £6,000,000 and from his taxes on manufactured articles he calculates that he will obtain £1.4,000,000. With this revenue he proposes to abolish the war taxes on food; but as the community is entitled to that relief in any case the reply to Mr. Chamberlain will be, "Thank you for nothing." But what of the £14,000,000 balance of revenue that remains? Into whose pocket is it intended that that shall go ? Evidently not the poorer class, as Mr. Chamberlain considers heir claims satisfied if their food does not CO21; hen a farthing more or a farthing less.

It has been said that the traveller by train is safer than he who walks in the public highway, and in some senses there is considerable truth in the remark. But the return of accidents and casualties on the railways in the United Kingdom during the six months to June 30th last certainly shows that, small as the percentage of lives lost on the railways is, it might be much smaller were the travellers to take greater care of themselves. Thus, during the six months, accidents to trains, rolling stock, permanent way, &2., caused the deaths of 4 and injury to 368 persons. But accidents to per- sons from other causes, including their own want of caution or misconduct, were responsible for the deaths of 339 people and injury to 990. In this category are to be found the accidents to passengers in alighting from or entering trains, and it is astonishing to note what a large pro- portion of them are recorded. Carelessnoss is generally the real cause of such accidents—or, at any rate, disregard, which has become habitual, of the warnings to "wait until the train stops "—and a similar comment may be made on the large number of casualties to persons while using level crossings. The railway train is obviously less dangerous to those who are in it than it is to those who are outside or are entering or leaving it; but, taking a broad view of the return, there is certainly no evidence that tie railway companies are themseluos directly responsible for the majority of the accidents which happen on their lines.

In each instance the defendants pleaded guilty, and were fined is. (kt.liand 10s. 6d. costs. MERSEY MISSION TO SEAMEN. Highly successful children's concerts were given inithe mission, Station-road, Runcorn, on Tuesday, 'Wednesday and Thursday evenings before crowded audiences. A cantata "The May festival" was creditably rendered by the ckildren and afterwards a miscellaneous programme was submitted, including instrumental selections by Misses Speakman, Johnson, Crowther, Whitley and Jukes, songs by Miss P. A DANGEROUS WIDNES LAD. At Liverpool Quarter Sessions on Tuesday, Samuel Duckham, aged fifteen, pleaded guilty to having, at Widnes, unlawfully and maliciously wounded a youth named Alfred Jones.—Mr. Morris, who appeared for the prosecutor, stated that the two lads worked together at the Widnes Foundry. At about four o'clock last Wednesday afternoon some rough play arose among a number of the young pe9ple working at the foundry. Someone threw a bag at prisoner, and prisoner threw it at prosecutor, who retaliated. Prisoner was heard to say somethingabout putting a knife through Jones. At aboutfive o'clock prisoner waited at tile foundry gate, and when the prosecutor came out he threw a. piece of iron at him, hitting him over the left eye. A nasty wound, about an inch in length, was caused, and an artery appeared to have been severed. It would, said counsel, be at least a week before prosecutor was all right.—The Chairman characterised the offence as a very serious and cruel one. If prisoner had been a few years older they would have sent him to gaol for a, long period. Theyhoped that it would be a serious warning to the prisoner, who would be imprisoned for one day, and would receive ten strokes of the birch rod

- , ALLEGED ASSAULT ON A RUNCORN GIRL. At the Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday, before Messrs. F. J. Norman (in the chair) and J. Pritchard, Francis Collins, labourer, Runcorn, was charged with having assaulted Ruth Percival (19), South Bank- terrace, Runcorn, on December Bth. Mr. H. J. Longton (Warrington) appeared for the complainant and the defendant was represented by Mr. J. W. Knowles (Widnes).—The facts were that his client was going to her aunt's house along a lonely place called the Holloway. The time was half-past five in the evening, and it was dark. At a place where there were no houses immediately about she met defendant going towards the railway station. In her own words he crouDhed, sprang towards her and tried to leg her down. He then forced her to the ground and putting his knees upon her chest, tried to puts red handkerchief into her mouth. She struggled and screamed, and when some- one came along the road defendant left her and ran away in the direction of the station.—Complainant bore out her solicitor's statement. She said he identified defendant from among five other men at the Police Station. Evidence of a conflicting nature was given and defGnclant giving a strong denial of the charge, the Chairman said there was a considerable doubt and they would give the defendant the benefit of it. (Applause.) Defendant.—Thank you. I have never molested the girl in my life.

RUNCORN SONS OF TEMPERANCE. In connection with the above a new cadet juvenile section was opened in Halton-road School room on Saturday evening last. The opening ceremony was con- ducted by Bro. John Brown of Weston, chief cadet officer Or the district, the folllwing officers being present—T. Cooke, P.G.W.P..T. J. Holt, district secre- tary, T. Myte, G.D. trustee, G. Powell, W.P., E. W. Key, P.W.P„ J. Walker, W.C., and. Bro. Armstrong who was appointed chief officer of the new cadet section and Bro. John Haddock who was appointed secretary. After the initation of the new cadets a short address was given by Bro. Brown, in which he pointed out that the section was a Sick Benefit Society as well as a teetotal one. He urged the members to stick to their temperance pledge and to influence other boys and girls to join the Order. Bro. Thomas Cooke also spoke and offered to give a Ist and 2nd prize respectively to the cadets who intro- duced the largest number of members during the next three months. Bro. Thomas Whyte followed and offered a 3rd prize. This section is the second one in Runcorn. It is in the hands of a good committee and has every prospect of being a success in the district.

WILL OF THE LATE MR. J. S. ECCLES. Probate of the will of Mr. Joseph Snape Eccles, cigar dealer, of 171, Windleshaw-road, St. Helens, Lancashire,who died on October 18, at the age of forty- nine, has been granted.to his brother, Mr. John Cross Eccles, solicitor, who values the estate at £5,009 17s. 7d. grop and £4,527 us. 11d. net. SUDDEN DEATH OF A SCHOOLGIRL. Annie Cox, aged six, a pupil at Windle Schools, St. Helens, was unable to go to school on Thursday to receive a prize for never being absent from school for a. year, and when the other children ran home to 14, Stanley-street, they took the prize upstairs, but were unable to wake her. The girl's father then went, and was horrified to find the child dead. She had suffered from sickness and vomiting during the previous night.

The quarterly meeting of the ministers and officers of the Wesleyan Churches comprised in the Warring- ton Circuit was held at Bold-street on Thursday. About seventy sat down in the sahoolroom to a tea which had been abundantly prepared and tastefully spread by various ladies of the congregation to whom a hearty vote of thanks was accorded. After tea the business was conducted under the presidency of the Rev. G. H. Carman prayer being offered by Rev, A. W. Rees. The financial statement showed a small balance in hand and the numerical statement,a small decrease which occasioned a discussion in which part was taken by the Revs. J. Howard, G. H. Carnson, W, C. J. Neville and Messrs. Meldrum and Lamplugh, Thanks were tendered to Messrs. G. Weaver and J. G. Withinshaw for their services as Circuit Stewards and they were reappointed. The following appoint- ments were also made : —Secretary : Mr, W, Silcock ; Circuit Chapel Secretary; Mr. A. H. Dunn: Educa- tional-Secretary, Rev. W. C. J. Neville: Treasurer, Circuit travelling Fund, Mr. R. G, Hen'shall. The local preachers were thanked for their services, Mr, J. Bailey responding on their behalf. Auditors were appointed for Foreign Missionary accounts and a Committee appointed to organize a canvass of the Circuit to further arouse enthusiasm in Missionary enterprise. Sanction was given for a special appeal to be made in March in all the churches on behalf of the British and Foreign Bible Society. The premises at Ellesmere-street having become inadequate for the present congregation and Sunday school a scheme to build a School Chapel was presented which the meet- ing heartily accepted, recognizing the pressing need of the case. A. committee was formed to make arrange- ments for the reception of the district meeting which is to meet in Warrington fin May, 1904. The tone of the meeting was optimistic and of a high spiritual order. Mr. H. Thornton and;Temperance Work. The quarterly meeting of the Lancashire and Cheshire Counties Band of Hope Union was held on Saturday at Radcliffe. Mr. Henry Thornton, of War- rington, presided over a meeting of the executive in the afternoon. A discussion took place with regard to the erection of the building in Deansgate, Manchester, for the Union's headquarters. It appeared that half of the z£15,000 required for this purpose, and for the scientific temperance lectures in day schools, had been either raised or definitely premised, but as it is impossible to complete the fund this year the committee were instructed to centinue the scheme during 1904. The Chairman renewed his offer to contribute 500 to the fund on the condition that the whole of the sum was raised within a specified time. Numer- ous meetings. extending over a week, were arranged in connection with the annual conference of the Union to be held in Manchester next February. The following resolution was unanimously adopted: "That this executive, representing 81 towns and dis- trict societies, and upwards of 270,000 members, pro- tests strongly against any proposal (a) to provide compensation for the non-renewal of licences, and (b) to limit the discretionary powers of licensing magis- trates, and pledges itself to strenuously resist any measure having for its object the pro- vision of such compensation or limitations."— A conference was afterwards held, presided over by . • Mr. J. • ir -13 - K ILL ED ON IS IRTHDAI Joseph Buckley, single, aged forty-nine, of 381, Fleet- lane, St. Helens, died early on Thursday morning from injuries. Buckley was engaged on the pit brow at, Ashton's Green Colliery on Wednesday morning, when he was caught between two railway waggons unde4 the screens. Buckley was to have celebrated his fairty- ninth birthday on Thursday. BURGLARY AT PRESCOT. At Liverpool Quarter Sessions, on Tuesday, JA, Quickley, aged eighteen, labourer, was charged NNIN having, at Prescot, on the 26th ult., broken into aDif entered the dwelling-house of George William Unwire and stolen therefrom one watch and chain, two snits of clothes, and a quantity of other goods.—Mr. Maxwell prosecuted,and stated that prosecutor lived in Carlton- street, Prescat. At seven o'clock on the morning of the Nth ult., he locked up his house and went to his work. At noon he returned and found that the premises had been broken into and several articles stolen. The prisoner had pawned certain of the articles. He now pleaded guilty. There was nothing against him so far as the police records went.—He was sent to gaol for six calendar months. RUN.A.W AY APPRENTICE'S ADVENTURES. Harry Critchley, a pawnbroker's apprentice, eighteen years of age, found himself in a serious Position at St. Helens Police Court on Monday, when he was sent to gaol for two months' hard labour. Mr. James Cook, who prosecuted. said Critchley was apprenticed to Messrs. B. A. Dromgoole and Co. On August 15 last he was left by Mr. Austin Dromgoole to lock up the money, &c., at the Westfield-street shop. He telephoned to the Liverpool-road shop for an overcoat, and went off with £5B and goods of a total value of £6O 12s. 6d. He visited Glasgow, and after spending all the money left the Argyle Hotel, Glasgow,without paying

IMPUDENT SWINDLE AT ST. HELENS. At the Liverpool Quarter Sessions on Tuesday Margaret Ford, aged 32, pleaded not guilty to having, on the 12th inst, at St. Helens, stolen 9s. .9d. and two bottles of lemonade from Owen Brady by means of a. trick.--From. the statement of Mr. Greaves Lord. who prosecuted, and from the evidence, it appeared that just before eleven o'clock on the night of the 12th inst., prisoner accompanied by another woman, went into the prosecutor's public-house and asked for two bottles of lemondade. She produced a bright coin, saying it was. half a sovereign. The prosecutor believed her and did not examine the coin, and gave her 9s. gd. change. After the women had left prosecutor discovered the supposed j half-sovereign was only si farthing. Prisoner was arrested, ! and on the way to the bridewell she said, " He was a ! silly-to give me Os. for a farthing." The jury found the prisoner guilty. She had a had record, and was sent 1;to prison for four calendar months.

Warrington Borough Police Court.
Miner Cases.

MONDAY.—Before the Mayor (in the chair), Alderman Smethurst, Councillor Thornton, Messrs. Birchen and Wright. THEFT BY A SoLDlEtt.—Michael Hogan. a soldier stationed at Orford Barracks, was charged with stealing from the barrack room at Orford Barracks a silver watch and white metalchain of the value of £2, the property of William C`onroy, comrade.—The Chief Constable said prosecutor left the watch in a box which was locked on November 20th. On the following day he found it had disappeared, and as the box was still locked it must have been opened by means of a dupli- cate key. A young man named George Chadwick was subeequently asked by the prisoner to pledge the watch for him, and he took it to Messrs. Jackson's shop. In consequence of police infoymation the watch wan " stopped " and prisoner was arrested. He at first denied the offence, but now pleaded guilty, stating that he committed the theft with the intention of being dis- charged from the army as he "did not like it." He had deserted once.—He was sent to gaol for a month. BREACH- OF THE PEACE.—For committing a breach of the peace by fighting in Win Wick-street, William Maughan, 85, roster-street, and William Allison, 52, Forshaw-street, were bound over in the sums, of ‘.1.,.5 each to keep the peace. DRUNK WHILST IN CHARGE OF A CHlLD.—Annie Jackson, Dolman's Yard, was fitted ss. and costs for having been drunk whilst in charge of a child on Satur- day night.—P.C. Clough proved the case. CRUELTY TO A HORSE.—Thomas Miller,Black Brook, ; Fearnhead, was summoned for having cruelly ill-treated a horse by working it whilst in an unfit condition on the 4th inst.—lnspector Gibson, R.S.P.C.A. said he was j in Wilderspool-road and saw the defendant driving a I grey mare attached to a spring cart. The animal was lame and moved with great difliculty.—P.C. Mriskett and Mr. Dixon, veterinary surgeon, having given evid- ence a fine of ss. and costs was imposed. At the Warrington County Petty Sessions on Wed- nesday, Edward Kelly, a tramp, was charged with wilfully setting fire to cornstacks, the property of James J. Brook, Mersey View Farm. Rixton, on the 9th inst.—The evidence showed that Mr. John Naylor, con- fectioner, Stamford-street, Warrington, was driving along Manchester-road, when he saw the prisoner run from behind a Dutch barn at the farm. Immediately afterwards the stacks burst into, flames and were destroyed.--When apprehended by P.C. Clarke prisoner admitted the offence.—He was remanded until Monday next.

div.head: PEN KETH.
div.p: PEN KETH.

A NARROW ESCAPE.—An exciting:, though un- pleasant adventure betel Richard Peniston, a time- keeper at Messrs. Tomlinson and Heywood's works, on Monday morning last. He was Making his way to the works at 5.30 a.m., to get there had to cross the canal at Fiddlers Ferry. By some means the bridge had been left open, and being unable to notice this in the dark, Peniston walked into the canal. The sides just at the bridge hole are faced with stone,and although he could swim, he had great diffi.culty in getting hold,hampered as he was by a heavy coat. As the hour was so carly,no one was about to lend assistance, but fortunately he managed to scramble out. The shock to him was very severe, and he has been off work the greater part of the 1 week.

The roof of a Roman Catholic chapel at Wellington, %Salop, suddenly collapsed and fell with a crash on Wednesday into the body of the building. A stained gins; window, several oil paintings, and the mission cross were destroyed. The damage is estimated at £3,000.

THE DANGERS OF UNPROTEgTED FIRES.

div.head: Strong Remarks by Coroner Brighouse.
div.p: Strong Remarks by Coroner Brighouse.
LEMSLATION THE ONLY REMEDY.

At inquest was conducted at the Police Station on Monday afternoon by Mr. S. Brighouse, County Coroner touching the death of Leonie Siliars Cawley, the four year-old child of Thornis wley, general labourer,2l Garabaldi-streat, who sustained fatal burns on Friday' last. . . _ _

Jane Annie Cawley, mother of the deceased,stated that at 2.15 on Priday afternoon she had occasion to leave the house to make a purchase at a shop close by, leaving the deceased and the baby in the kitchen. On her way to the shop she called at the house of 'Mrs. Slnittleworth, a neighbour, and, ask her to look after the children during her absence. On returning she was informed that &ceased had sustained burns. Later the child was taken to the Infirmary and she told witness that she was playing with the fire when her clothing balight.- Mrs. Shuttleworth, 36 Garabaldi-street, said that at the reques',, of the last witness she went to the house and, taking up the baby, told deceased to follow her. When she got back to her own house she failed. to see anything.of the deceased 'and shortly afterwards heard that she had been burnt. Theresa Ancock, 23, Garabaldi-street, said that she was in the kitchen when she heard a loud knocking at the fire place of Cawley'S house next door. On going into the house she saw deceased with her clothing on fire. Se raised an 'alarm and with assistance, oxtinguishecFthe flames. Nurse' Griffiths said deceased was admitted to the Infirmary at three O'clock on Friday :Otero° on suffering from severe burns about the lower part of th e body and died at six o'clock. Addressing the jury the Coroner said he wanted to know what was going td be done to prevent these deaths from burning. At every similar inquest be held he intended to repeat some facts to see if he could not make an impression on the mothers og South Wes t Lancashire. The fact that these deaths were so frequent came to the notice of the Government who put them- selves into communication with the Coroners' Society, of London, of which he was a member. Through the assistance of that society they obtained statistics as to the number of deaths that took place in consequence of efficient fire guards not being provided, with the, result that it was found during the years 1899 and 1900 in- quests were held on the bodies of 1684 young children, -whose deaths had resulted from burns, and in 1425 of these cases the fire Which caused the burns was without. a guard. In consequence of that the Government com- municated with all the local governing bodies and notices were issued calling the attention of parents and guardians to the absolute necessity of provid- ing efficient fireguards. What was his own experience. Since October 13th he had held no fewer than eleven inquests on the bodies of young childrenwho had•died from burns, and he now quoted the police reports in severallof the cases, show- ing that the children were left. alone in rooms where there were unprotected fires. No one appreciated more than he did that a great many of these people had per- haps hard work to live, and they said they could not afford to buy a fire guard. He had previously pointed out that a guard could be obtained- for 2s. 6d., and this amount spread out over a year worked out at three farthings per week. It was no use talking to parents. It was like "water cn a duck's back." The only remedy was for the legislature to step in and pass an Act of Parliament making it an offence for parents to leave their children in a room where there wasan unprotected fire. A fine of 40s. and costs could be imposed for a -first offence, and for a second offence let the parents b Imprisoned. If the jury agreed with him he suggested that they should add a presentment to their_verdict that it was quite time the legislature stepped in and created the conduct he had referred to an offence. The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death" and the foreman (Mr. T. Walsh) said they had agreed to add the rider as suggested by the Coroner. They also went so far as to say that builders of cottage property might provide fireguards. In many cases they thought the conduct of parents amotlnted to culpable negligence.

div.head: PAUPER BEER AT LEIGH. A Versatile Priest.
div.p: PAUPER BEER AT LEIGH. A Versatile Priest.

Some extraordinary speeches were made at I'Vednes- day's meeting of the Leigh Board of Guardians on a motion by the Rev. W. H. Carr to rescind a resolution that tile inmates of the Workhouse be given the usual dinner on Christmas Day, including an allowance of beer.
--Mr. J. Cooke, an octogenarian, who seconded the resolution' said he had been a. teetotaler for 64 years And never had an ache,____ .../

The Rev. Father O'Neill said the true temperance man was he who could take his glass of anything and walk straight and never have a headache. That was himself! (Laughter.) If necessary, though over 60 years of age, he could dance an Trish jig or a Scotch flornpipe. lie believed that he .would be dead now if he were a teetotaler. (Loud laughter). This question, the priest added was as great a one as the fiscal policy. In conclusion Father O'Neill quoted: "Nmpires may totter and thrones may wane, But the p-utper s beer will ever reign." It was resolved by 20 votes to 12 that the paupers have their beer.

PATRIOTISM AND ELECTIONEERING.
MR. CHAMBERLAIN'S METHODS.

div.head: ANOTHER FORGOTTEN SPEECH.
div.p: ANOTHER FORGOTTEN SPEECH.

Colonial Support. IT has been Mr. Chamberlain's first move to try and represent the Colonies as unanimously in support of his schemes; indeed, he has told us they demand the scheme, and that unless we are prepared to grant it the Empire will fall to pieces. The object of this move was obvious. Once it could be shewn that the Colonies were unanimously demanding Pre- ference, all who opposed Mr. Chamberlain were necessarily enemies of the Colonies! His efforts to produce this demand resulted in one • of the ugliest incidents of his whole campaign. It is not surprising that Mr. Chamberlain' in publishing his speeches in volume form, has found it necessary to omit the speech which this incident called forth. Let us brefiy relate the facts. On May Itii and 28th Mr. Chamberlain made speeches in which he urged upon the people of this country the necessity of imposing taxes so as to be able to give a preference to the Colonies. He spoke as a member of' the Government and as Colonial Secretary. The ,Prime Minister did not take exception to those speeches, and apparently privately acquiesced in them. On June 6th the Colonal Office published a message from the Governor of New South Wales, who stated that "the New South Wales Government recognised the advantages of such preferential trading to Australia, and strongly supported Mr. Chamberlain's proposals." Further, the message expressed "great satisfaction at the declaration by the British Gwernment that every self-governing Colony should be secured in the free exercise of its right to enter into closer trade relations with the Mother Country." That was a message which Mr. Chamber- lain evidently thought would greatly strengthen his case. It *as quickly sent to the Press —an unusual course. Perhaps Mr. Chamber- lain expected other Colonies would follow suit with further messages in a similar strain. Had they done so his case for Preference would have been almost irresistible; but they did not do so. Indeed, it seems somewhat doubtful how this New South Wales message was secured. The Governor was not authorised to send the message. The Government of New South Wales had no power to support such a policy, by granting preferential tariffs to British produce; this power is reserved to the Federal Government. The isolated message from New South Wales may or may not have been prompted by Mr. Chamberlain, but it has all the appearance of his authorship. A latter message from the Premier of New South Wales stated that the speeches of Mr. Cham- berlain and Mr. Balfour were the cause of the "great satisfaction " referred to in the message. The whole matter was brought before Parlia- ment on a motion for the adjournment of the House moved by Sir Henry Campbell-Banner- man on June 17th. The motion was brought forward to draw attention to "the misunder- standing created in the minds of the Govern- ment of New South Wales by the speeches of the Prime Minister and the Colonial Secretary." In the course of the debate it became abundantly clear that the Prime Minister was anxious to escape from any responsibility for a policy of Preference, with- out having to publicly disown the Colonial Secretary. As for Mr. Chamberlain, he ignored the whole question, and devoted Ins remarks to the relations between Canada and Germany! Only at the end of his speech id he make any reference to a general policy of Preference, and then he said:

The right hon. gentleman oppdsite is afraid lest the Colonies should be disappointed. Sir, the Colonies have been disappointed with our policy hitherto, is it we who raise the question ? No, it is they. They raised it, and not one Colony alone; every individual Colony raised it, by the mouth of its -Prime Minister at the recent conference, when a resolution was unanimously passed asking his Majesty's Government to call attention to this matter, to consider the matter, and see if they could do something to meet the desire of the Colonies for this closer commercial union, which in my heart and soul I believe is absolutely essential if hereafter you are to have that closer federal union I believe to be the real destiny of the British race, and with- out which the. Empire will fall to pieces and disjointed atoms.

There you have again the attempt to represent the Colonies . as. unanimously demanding Preference, and the maintenance of the Empire depending upon the granting of that demand. As to what • took place at the Colonial Conference, Mr. Chamberlain has refused to have the full report published. As to whether the Colonial Premiers unanimously demanded Preference, although other resolu- tions passed at the Confenuce were published, no such resolution has as yet appeared. All we know is that the Canadian :preference was declared to be a failure. According to a later speech by Mr. Chamberlain at the Constitutional Club on June 26th, it was he who suggested a Preferential trading 'to the Premiers, and the Premiers promised to urge upon their respective Governments the desir- ability of giving a preference to British goods. As to whether the Empire will fall into pieces and disjointed atoms, we know, according to the published report, that the Colonial Premiers declared that their Govern- ments were quite capable of looking after their own interests. In the report of the Colonial Conference Blue-,book is the following: In connection with the discussion of pre- ferential trade, the Conference also considered the point raised by the Commonwealth Govern- ment as to the possibility of the Colonies losing the most-favoured-nation treatment in foreign countries in the event of their giving a tariff preference to British goods. As, however, the exports from the Colonies to foreign countries are almost exclusively articles of food or raw materials for various industries, the possibility of discriminating against them in foreign markets was not regarded as serious; and as the exports . from the foreign countries to the Colonies are mainly manufactured articles, it was recognised that if such discrimination did take place the Colonies have an effective remedy in their own hands.

The above resolution, about which there is no doubt, effectively disposes of all Mr. Chamber- lain's alarms. The Colonies are independent of help in matters of trade as well as of Government. Do not let us, therefore, be drawn away from Free Traci, on the plea that the Colonies demand a Preference. Mr. Chamberlain's desire for the 'welfare of the Empire is almost as deep as his spurious desire for social reforms and Old-Age Pensions. About the year 1895, Mr. Chamberlain used to was as pathetic over the lot of the poor as he now grows eloquent over the fate of the Empire and British trade. Once snugly ensconced in office, the Empire and trade wguld be as quickly fagotten as the poor were in 1895. Mr. Chamberlain is great at vote- catching, but he has played the game once too often.
The Examiner, Saturday December 19, 1903..

div.head: WARRINGTON SAVINGS BANK.
div.p: WARRINGTON SAVINGS BANK.
Satisfactory Progress.
The Warrington Savings Bank_ continues to make

satisfac to. ry progress. This was the burden of the re- port presented at a meeting of trustees and managers, held at the Bank premises, on Tuesday morning. Mr. William Long presided and there werd also present : Mr. John Geddes (vice chairman), Messrs. F. Monks, George Dakin, Mimes Hepherd, H. Roberts. C. Jackson Holmes, J. Rymer Young, C. White (Trustees), Revs. Canon Willis, Rev. William Bracecamp, Rev. J. Davies, Rev. J. F. Matthews, Dr. Fox, Councillor Craik, Messrs. T. Birchall, John Dewhurst, -John Harrison, C. D. Parkinson, E. Richardson, E. Woods, (managers) and Thomas Tunstall (actuary).
THE CoMMITsTEE OF MANAGEMENT'S REPORT

In presenting the general statement of accounts of the bank for the year ended 20th November, 1903, the Committee of Management state that they have much pleasure in drawing attention to the very satisfactory progress of the blis.ness of the bank. 969 new and re- newed accounts have been opened during the year, making the total number of depositors 13,636, 38,268 transactions vi'ere recorded as compared with. 426,641 last year; showing an increase of 1627. £2,502 us lid has. been invested for depositors during the year in con- solidated stock. The amount now due to depositors is £355,192 3s 3d, in addition to which there are

investments on:their behalf to the extent of £16,482 Os 2d in stock. The assets of the 'bank are £361,742 13s 9d, showing a surplus of £6,550 9s 6d,after deducting the whole amount due to depositors. The National Debt Commissioners hold on behalf of the Institution a sum of £357,162 5s 7d, which is considerably in excess of the total liabilities. The continued steady increase in the amount due to depositors and in the number of transactions, is a most gratifying feature of the work of the bank. The greater proportion of the transactions are of small amounts, which shews that the bank is taken advantage of by the class of depositors for whose benefit the Institution was established in the year 1818. There are 5,880 depositors, whose accounts do not exceed one pound.
SPEECH BY THE CHAIRMAN.

The CHAIRMAN, in moving the adoption of the report, observed that the account of their year's work was a record of which none of them were ashamed. It showed that the bank was doing the good work for which it was originally established. He was loth to put any more figures before them, but he would like to show the record of the bank as taken in the years 1883, 1893, and 1903, so as to illustrate the steady progress made during those decades. In 1883 the depositors numbered 9,058; 1893, 10,793; and in 1903, 13,636; a total increase of over 1,000: The amount due to depositors had grown' from £279,560 in 1883, to '£203,000 in 1893, and £355,000 In 1903. The number of transactions—and that was, to his thinking, one of the main points in considering the value of a bank—was 13,373 in 1883,17,584 in 1893, and 28,265 in 1903,which showed a great increase. The amounts received had gone up from,£4o,ooo in 1833 to £70,000 in 1893 and £73,000 in 1903, and the amount paid had increased from £41,800 in 1883, and £54,800 in 1893 to £78,300 in 1903. (Hear, hear.) There was one point he wished to emphasize in the report, and that was that there had been 968 new accounts opened in the year and that the transactions, as had already been stated, had increased to 28,268. (Hear, hear.) The steady increase was a most gratifying feature, and the number of very small aceounts showed that the:bank was being taken advantagel of by those for whose benefit it was originally intended. He only wished that the words spoken at that meeting might go forth amongst the labouring population. If they could draw more savings into the bank instead of them going into the public-house it would be very much to the advantage of Warrington and its career. (Hear, hear.) Mr. GEDDES seconded.

The Rev. J. DAVIES asked a question with reference to the number of closed account which totalled up to 584. Were the accounts principally closed about Walking Day, and what were the reasons for the with- drawals?

The ACTUARY said it would be very difficult to give the reasons, but the withdrawals were largely due to removals from the district and matters of that sort. There was no special time which marked the with- drawals, and he quoted the figures for each month of the year, which showed that the numbers of withdrawals were general throughout the year. The Rev. J. F. MATTHEW s inquired if the withdrawals were of the small deposit class. The ACTUARY : They belong to all @lasses. It is quite general. _ _
The motion was then carried unanimously. THE COMMITTEE THANKED.

Mr. HENRY ROBERTS proposed the adoption of the report of the Committee of Management, and a vote of thanks to the committee for their valuable services during the year. He observed that the figures proved very 7conclqsively two things, first, that the rate of progress of tile last ten years was far in excess of any previous decade and secondly, that the principle of thrift—which, had been advocated so often and so strenuously at these meetings—had taken hold more generally than had ever previously been the case. The trustees and managers could congratulate themselves on those two important facts. The second portion of the resolution referred to the services of the Committee of Management, who deserved very hearty and sincere thanks. The fact that there was, in connec- tion with that institution, as in the many other institu- tion which had made our country famous, a large amount of the voluntary work for which there was no recom- pense except the recompense of a good conscience and the satisfaction of feeling that one was doing some- thing for those wholcould not do everything possible for themselves, was in itself a matter for congratulation. The gentlemen named in his resolution were fully en- titled to that satisfaction. If it were not for their efforts, voluntarily given, the- progress of that institu- tion could not be anything. like so effective as it was. (Hear, hear.) The RECTOR seconded the resolution, and endorsed the remarks of Mr. Roberts. He trusted that what the Chairman had said would be a great encouragement to the public. The motion was unanimously passed. ELECTION OF CHAIRMAN AND VICE-CHAIRMAN.

Mr. F. MONKS proposed that Mr. Long be re-elected chairman, and Mr. Geddes vice-chairman. No words of his, he said, were needed to comm ad the resolution, (Hear, hear). Mr. DEWHURST seconded, and remarked that that institution ought to have the best support of the Dimple of Warrington. (Hear, hear.) The fact that they had had the Chairman and Vice-Chairman at the head of affairg for a long period gave a certain amount of continuity to the work of the bank.

The motion was unanimously agreed to. Mr. LONG rettuned thanks on behalf of himself and Mr. Geddes. tie said it was a pleasure to him to do what he could for the bank, the interests of which he had very much at heart. If he had not got such an able deputy he would not dare to preside over the work of management.

div.p: HARRIERS.

WARRINGTON v. SANKEY. I The above run took place from the Bridge Inn on Saturday last. This important fixture was looked to with much interest, bin owing to several of the War- : rington Harriers' best runners not being available it ; was only a poor race. Seven of 'Warrington and 25 of ;. Sankey faced the starter, and just after the, start C. Dagnall, one of Warrington Harriers, fell on soruesetts and cut, his knee badly, thus spoiling Warrington's i,chance. of winning. After going through Arpley , meadows and ronnd by Moore it was seen that C. ;i. Straw, Warrington, was leading and he finally won by five hundred yards, followed by S. Parsonage,of Sankey, and several more of his club. Sankey thus winning easily. The return fixture will be of a more even character, as Warrington Hari ,l's will have a full terun.

div.head: WENT TO HIS DEAtil SINGING
div.p: WENT TO HIS DEAtil SINGING

1 Hanley is still excited over the sensational accident which occurred there on •Saturday, by which a young maw named Holland. while walking along the street,Was ,swallowed up in the shaft of a disused coalpit. At a meeting of the town council on Tuesday Councillor Harrison stated that Holland was singing Sankey's hymn, "When the roll is called lip yonder I will be there," and he had just finished the refrain when the crust of the shaft caved in and he disappeared. I Miss Emma Austin Frye, an elderly lady, of Ilford, whilst carrying a teapot from the dining-room to the kitchen on Tuesday, in the dark walked through the cellar doorwey, and fell to the bottom of the stairs. Death was instantaneous.

div.head: Bewsay Ward Eltetions.
div.p: Bewsay Ward Eltetions.

Sir,—The recent Bewsey ward elections are now -matters of history but there is one incident about them which will ever keep their memory fresh in the minds of church people resident within the ward. For the 'first time in the history of electioneering in the ward the polling booth has been held in a place reserved for Divine Worship, and, whoever is responsible for it has given great offence and . infinite sorrow to those worshippin,, in it. Why this place should have been singled out for the purpose is beyond my comprehen- sion seeing that there are several places in the ward far more suitable and appropriate to the purpose. Is there denomination in the town who would have let their church or chapel for such a purpose? How delicious it seems to me to hold two elections on consecutive Mondays and to administer Holy Communion on the intervening Sabbath in the same place—truly it is a strange way to welcome the advent of the Christian year. Instead of rejoicing many of the little congre- gation are filled with anger at the pollution of their little sanctuary and wish to know who is the respon- sible party in the matter. I remain yours &c., AN ALL SAINTS' PARISHIONER.

div.head: Inquiry and Other Things.
div.p: The Inquiry and Other Things.

Sir,—Your correspondent"lona,"has in his two recent letters advanced suggestions and opinions that commend themselves to all right-minded people, because of his reasonable and commonsense view of the difficulties agitating the public mind just now and the easiest way out of them. So much that is contradictory has been said and written that one sometimes wonders where we are in the matter, and as for the truth and nothing but the truth is there any such thing? Now that the inquiry is on the carpet we may reason- ably hope that one 'phase of the agitation is within measurable distance of the end. And we naturally ask ourselves what those people think who said "there never would be an inquiry, the Non-Traders don't want , an inquiry," who threatened legal proceedings and played the game of " bluff " at election time, to throw the I voters off the main issue and gain a victory by election- eering methods which are—their own. It is quite evident that the wish was father to the thought. It is not possible to think of these things without thinking of Mr. H. Roberts in connection with them and realizing that he has been ill-advised in again com- ing to the front. He should "Let the sleeping dog lie," and be thankful. Nothing that he can say or do, either directly or indirectly, will convince the much-quoted "ratepayer" that a man engaged in his class of business ought to be a town councillor- much less a Mayor of the Borough. The wonder is that for years the dual position was tolerated, and might have continued to be so even now, but for the stand taken by Mr. Dodds, who if he has done nothing else.has put a stop to members of the Corporation trading with themselves. Much has been said about Mr. Roberts being "ousted out of public life." To my mind, he ousted himself out, and his best friends at the time of his resignation, wished that he would stand firm and face it out and not turn tail. He is too much given to taking things to himself personally, forgetting that public men live in a fierce light, have to submit to criticism and that after all principle is the chief thing. Personal feeling in connection with public matters ought to count for very little. The man is only the nieans to an end, and should forget himself and his own interest, serving the public faithfully and well to the 1 best of his ability, his reward being the consciousness ' of having done what is right, without fear or favour! or profit.—l am, yours Scc. • STILL ANOTHER RATEPAYER.

div.head: Poor Law Administration.
div.p: Poor Law Administration.

Sir,—Several guardians called my attention on Wed- nesday to a statement by Mr. Councillor James Evans conveying to ratepayers the impression "that out of each shilling paid for relief of the poor ninepence went in salaries" Upon subsequent reference I find Mr. Evans to be thus reported—" as to poor law adminis- tration it wasa shame that for every shilling obtained for that cause ninepence was spent in working the law." Other disbursements may have been on the mind of Mr. Evans inclusive of executive outlay. Even so although an old reader of poor law literature and statistics I have not before read or Leard of three fourths of con- tributions for poor law purposes being spent as Mr. Evans suggests. lam told the impression left on the minds of the public by the words used is that for each shilling of the rate they pay for the relief of the poor ninepence goes to salaries. If so a nearer approach to accuracy is due to the ratepayers. The local press psually publish what may be called the Union Budget. From that source the public learn the details of outlay by the guardians,under 30 different heads, in the corres- ponding half of the previous financial year and under the same heads the estimated contributions by Parishes for the following half year. The total outlay in the half year ending at Lady Day, 1903, was £10,700 is. 9d. The total of estimates for the present half-year was £10,874. Of this latter sum £5,731, say fivepence halfpenny in the 2on the rateable value, is collected by the overseers of the County Borough. The average of Union calls made upon them may be estimated at six- pence half-yearly, equal to a shilling yearly. ft is somewhat hard on the poor to include with the "rate for the relief of the poor" the important items of vaccination, registration, assessment expenses, sub- scriptions to hospitals, nursing associations, etc, yet such are included. It is reasonable to say of medical and nursing salaries (I remember when one nurse only was needed at our Workhouse Infirmary—their number is now in the teens)that medical and nursing servicesare, 4equally with sick diet and othernecessaries, expenditure far the relief ofithe poor. It is also reasonable to say of salaries paid to the school and industrial teachers, combining instruction with profitable ser- Tice, that such services are relief to the poor. I do not, however, propose to exclude such outlay from the calculations. Inclusive of all such the proportion of the £5,731 or of the average sixpence in the £ applied to salaries is less than one halfpenny in the shilling or for a whole year is less than one penny in the shilling. If we exclude contributions obtained from other sources than rates, and monies recovered whereby outlay for salaries charged upon the rates is reduced, a penny in the shilling for a half year, or twopence for a year, would still be the probable maximum. Bewsey Chambers. 17th December.
J. C. SUTTON.

div.head: MUNICIPAL ELECTION SEQUEL. Alleged Bribery in Bewsey Ward.
div.p: MUNICIPAL ELECTION SEQUEL. Alleged Bribery in Bewsey Ward.
THE HEARING ADJOURNED.

There was a large attendance of the general public af the Warrington Police Court yesterday, when a case 0, alleged bribery against Councillor Samuel Gough, 105 Winwick-street, who successfully contested Bewsey Ward at a recent by-election, was down for hearing. Mr. F. Monks presided over the Bench, the other magis- trates present being : —The Mayor, Alderman Smethurst, -Councillor Thornton, Messrs. Hepherd, Wright and Young. Immediately on the opening of the Court, Mr. A. Browne,who has charge of the prosecution on behalf of Mr. E. A. Sanders,l2,Arthur-street,said that in the case of Sanders v. Gough which was a summons for alleged bribery at a recent election in Bewsey Ward, his friend Mr. Wallhead, who was representing the defendant, in- formed him on Thursday that he could not possibly prepare the defence for that day and suggested an adjournment. On consideration, and having had an interview with the magistrates' clerk who thought it was only reasonable, seeing that the summons was served on Wednesday, that an adjournment should be granted, prosecutor had decided to consent to an adjournment to a special day and he suggested Wed- nesday next. The case was accordingly adjourned until Wednesday.

Messrs. Beresford and Co., the well-known brush manufacturers, aye making a special extra display of Christmas novelties this season. For this purpose they have secured 52 Church-street,in addition to their oldes- tablishment,77,Church-street,Liverpool.The large window at 52, Ctturch-street, is exceptionally attraztive,having -very fine display of dressing bags ladies fitted blouse cases, purses, card, letter, cigar and cigarette cases in sealskin, crocodile, and lizard skins, all of latest designs, and in the newest art shades; also a fine selec- tion with hall-marked gold and silver mounts. A feature with Messrs. Beresfords is that their dressing bags and cases are fitted with Sheffield cutlery. A similar show on a smaller scale in one of the windows at 77, Church- street,proves most attractive, while the other window is devoted to brushes of their own manufacture. The' new toilet sets of dire finest African ivory flle deserving of special attention this season for those who desire .a most enduring and useful present at a moderate cost, while those in silver and ebony make most,- desirable presents for those who do not wish the more luxurious ivory sets. A suitable present for a gentleman is a pair of Ivory, Silver or Ebony Military Hair Brushes in a case of which there is a fine selection.—Altogether one would be wise in viewing Messrs. Beresfords superb Stock, who wish to secure Christmas Gifts up-to-date, taSteful, and of the utmost utility. -

div.head: LOCAL NEWS.
div.p: LOCAL NEWS.
(Continued from page 5).

Personal. Captain J. W. II Silverthorne, who was for five years adjutant of the South Lancashire Voluntbers and was afterwards adjutant of Lancashire Veterans in the Royal Reserve Regiment, has just vacated a similar appointment in the Royal Garrison Regiment at Malta. The Employment of Children.

At a meeting of the Watch Committee on Thursday the byelaws in connection with the Employment of Children Act, 1903 were formally adopted. One of the most important clauses reads as follows :—" No person under the age of 10 shall be employed in or carry on street trading after 8 o'clock in the evening, between the Ist of October and 31st March, or after 9 in the evening, between the Ist of April and 30th September." Fatality at Orford Tannery. - - - - -

At 2..45 yesterday morning James Leigh, aged 35, 29, Victoria-street, died in the Infirmary from a fractured skull. A.bout ten o'clock on Thursday morning deceased and a man named James Nairn were tightening a crane which was fastened by a wire rope to the beams of a building in course of erection at Messrs. Mortimer and Company's tannery, Orford. They were doing this by means of a pole, when the rope slipped, causing the pole to swing round and strike the decessed and Nairn on the head. Assistance was at hand and- the men were at once taken to the Infirmary. After his injuries had been attended, to Nairn was taken home and is pregrnsing satisfactorily. Leigh unfortunately succumbed at the time stated. He leaves a widow and several children. Spiritualism.

On Sunday at the Spiritualist Hall, Bewsey-street, Mr. J. Kay spoke on "Man in harmony with Deity," and on Monday evening Miss O'Neill, of Pendleton, -paid her first visit to Warrington, and gave a large number of clairvoyant descriptions, being successfnl in the majority of cases in obtaining recognition. On Wednesday evening, Professor Timson, F.8.P.5., phrenologist, hypnotist, brain. specialist &c., of Leices- ter, addressed a good audience on "Psychic Science and religious superstitions." The speaker dwelt on the wonderful structure of man, comparing his various ! parts with the earth, his honey formation correspond- I ing with the rocks, his flesh, muscles, &c., with the 1 vegetable kingdom, and his psychic or nervous system I with the magnetic condition of the earth; thus show- ing the harmony of creation. Man was a trinity in unity—body, soul, and spirit. The psychic portion of man's nature could ,not be discovered by the, anatomist or the chemist, but was an undoubted fact. The lecturer made a strong appeal to his hearers' to cultivate this most important part of their nature. I His remarks met with • evident appreciation and at ! the close lie was loudly applauded. Mr. Timson con- cluded by giving a number of brief but interesting ' phrenological and psychic delineations of members of the ,audience. Mr. W. J. G-rindley, of Chester, is announced as the speaker for to-morrow, and Mrs. A. Williams will give clairvoyance on Monday night. Warrington Board of Guardians. An interim meeting of this Board was held on Wednesday morning under the presidency of Mr. A. Brooks. There were also present :—Rev., Father Wilson, Mrs. Clay, Messss. T. H. Ashcroft, S. Davies, William Houghton, A. .T. Jolley, A. Jolley, G.Mather, G. Pilling, .T. Payton, J. Turton and the Clerk (Mr. C. . Sutten).—The Clerk stated that it had been suggested ' in the country Board room that morning that an alteration of the relieving officers' districts be made.l The proposal was to add to Mr. Auk-land's district, ' which was a very small one, the district of Winwick and some other adjoining parish,and thus relieve Mr. Bowes' district. He (the clerk) was instructed to call a special meeting that day month to consider the I matter.—The Chairman: I suppose you have got all instructions from the country board ?—The Clerk replied in the affirmative and said they did not Com- mit any of the members. It was simply a matter for consideration.—The Padgate Schools Committee recommended that Mr. and Mrs. Yates; of Radcliffe be appointed tailor and foster parents of number 1 home. The resignation of Miss Roberts (nurse and general assistant) was accepted, and it was agreed to interview suggested candidates for the post at the next meeting. These minutes were confirmed, on the proposition of Mr. Ashcroft, seconded by Mr. Mather. —The resignation of Miss Stringer as probationer • nurse was accepted.—The Clerk stated that he had received a latter from one of the inspectors of the Local. Government Board, asking him and the Chair- . man of the Board and the vaccination officers to meet him at his (the Clerk's) office at 11.30 on Thursday morning, to consider what steps the Board were taking with a view to preventing the spread of smallpox. He (the Clerk) had arranged a meeting.—This was all the business. The Priory School, Warrington. _

On Thursday evening the prize distribution and concert by the pupils was held in connection with. the . Misses Williams's School,the Priory, St. Austin's-lane. . The Co-operative Hall, Sankey-street, in which the function took place, was well filled with the parents. and friends of the pupils and others interested. Miss ' Williams opened the proceedings with a few remarks and particulars upon the progress and efficiency of the school and the results of the various examinations , &c., and gr. E. 3. Hall distributed the prizes after an interesting little'spbech in which he dwelt upon the great importance to be attached to the study of grammar as a social equipment. The following is a list of winners of prizes and certificates : Edith Cole, sixth class prize ; Constance Hall, fifth I class prize and Oxford local certificate; Aida Clarke, Agatha Jortes,fotirth class prizes ; Ida Haddock, third class prize; May Tinnion, second class prize; Muriel Matthews,first class prize; Reggie Tinnion, lower first prize ; Adalsherwood, examination and good conduct prizes; Lucy Skinner, conduct prize and Oxford local certificate ; Alys Walshe, attendance prize ; Mabel Crampton, attendance prize ; Dora Roberts, attendance prize.; Lucy Percival, French prize; Ida Silcock, music prize; Nellie Taylor, Oxford local certificate ; Dorothy Hall, music certificate from Trinity. College, London ; Clarice Newall, music • certificate from Incorporated Society of Musicians ; Dorothy Truslove, music certi- ficate .from Incorporated Society of Musicians. The entertainment whichifollowed consisted of piano- forte solos and duets, songs, and conterted vocal pieces by present and past pupils of the school; the second part of the programme being taken up with the performance of the very pretty operetta, founded on the legend of The Briar Rose, by Thomas Facer. The list of characters in this little musical' play found pleasant and edifying employment for a considerable number of pupils whose united efforts in singing and play-acting reflected high credit upon the training received at the hands of the Misses Williams. Good Templar Convention.

The December Session of the No. 1 South-West Lancashire Convention was held in the Primitive Methodist Chapel, Bamfurlong, representatives being present from Ashton, Leigh, -Hindley, Wigan, War- rington and Earlestown. Bro Parr, C.O.T. opened the session, and the usual order of business was gone through. The Secretary (Bro. Smith) in his report said that the. Lodges in the Convention were in a fairly-prosperous condition and that the' visitors appointed by the convention were doing their work in a very 'satisfactory manner. He called attention to the Whittaker-Sherwell compensation scheme now beforethe country and urged upon the representatives to bring the matter before their lodges and to do all in their power to influence their friends to take up a defiant attitude against the State having anything to do with compensation to the "trade." The reports from the various lodges were very satisfactory, although there was room for improvement in a few cases. The reports from the juvenile temples shewed that some very good work was being done in this branch of the work especially at Ashton and Warrington. It was resolved that a paper be written on the Whittaker- Shervrell Manifesto to be read at the next session of the convention. Invitations to hold the February session were received from Wigan and Warrington and on the vote being taken Wigan was selected. A good tea was provided by the members of the Ray of Hope Lodge for the visitors, after which a public meeting was held. Bro. Clarke,. C. C. Earlestown. occupied the chait and addresses were delivered by Bro. J. Parr, • C.C.T. Leigh, and Bro. F. Merlin, C. Electoral Superintendent, Warrington. Several items of music and recitations were rendered during the evening--At the evening meeting the following resolu- tion was put to the meeting and adopted.
