The Confirmation at St. Paul's Church.

- _ Owing to the dlness of the Suffragan Bishop of Liverpool (Dr. Royston) the confirmation service which he was to have conducted in St. Paul's Church to-day (Saturday) has been postponed until December 27th.
Brick-street Mission Band of Hope Society.

The third entertainment of the season in connection with the above was held on Tuesday evening, about 200 members being present. Mr. James Shaw (the president of the society) was in the chair and gave a very encouraging addre. ss. Recitations were given by Misses Martha Riley Mice Starkey, Alice Harding, ' Lily Woodhouse, Ethel Wright, Hannah Riley, and E. H. Bibby, and Masters William Wilson, *John H. Bibby, and Robert Ellison. Miss M. Gallop was the , soloist, and she and Miss H. Hill very ably rendered , a duet. Mr. W. Tomkinson contributed several gramaphone selections which were highly appreciated. The meeting concluded with a sketch entitled " Daddy's Pledge" which was very kindly given by friends from Friars' Green Band of Hone Society. The Soldiers' Memorial. A meeting of the Executive Committee appointed to raise funds for a memorial to the South Lancashire Regiment (Line, Militia, and Volunteers) for their services in South • Africa was held at the Town Hall on Monday last, the Mayor presiding. The committee resolved to raise,if possible,the sum of £1,500 for the proposed Memorial towards which the officers and men of the Regiment have already subscribed about £3OO. Major Roome and the Town Clerk were requested to draw up a statement and application for funds, and other preliminary details were discussed and settled. Several letters were read from members regretting their inability to attend the meeting. Colonel Reid Walker wrote to explain that his reason for consider- ing that it was premature to invite Mr. Alfred Drury, A.R.A., to submit a sketch of the proposed statue was that the Committee should wait until some idea of the amount they would have to expend could be obtained, and as the inhabitants of Widnes and St. Helens would be invited to subscribe they would, he presumed, have to be consulted. He added that he would be most pleased if the committee could see their way to ask Mr. Drury to carry out the work.

Debate on " Smoking." The Fairfield Literary and Debating Society held their usual fortnightly meeting on Monday evening last. The subject for discussion was "Smoking." Mr. John Young introduced the subject by reading a very carefully prepared and interesting paper, show- ing chiefly from a doctor's standpoint the detrimental effect smoking has upon the system. He argued that if smoking was bad for the youth it certainly followed that it must be as bad for the man, and finally by comparing England with other countries in which smoking is indulged in to excess he. moved the-follow- ing resolution, viz. :—" That as smoking is not bene- ficial to the system it should be discour- aged." Mr. E. Haigh opened the defence for the smoker's cause. 'He contended that if smoking was so detrimental to the system of a man it would make itself more apparent than it does. Men smoked and enjoyed their pipes, and unless some very good reasons were found this privilege should not be taken away from them. In an amendment he proposed he agreed that boys under the age of eighteen should not be allowed to smoke; that the sale of cheap cigarettes should be restricted by law, and that moderate smoking was not sufficiently detrimental to the health of a man to cause active steps to be taken for its discouragement. —After a warm • discussion on the subject, the Rev. A. S. Cameron summed the two sides up, and on a vote being taken it was found that the majority were in favour of the working man being allowed to enjoy his pipe in peace.

div.head: FISCAL PROBLEM.
div.p: THE FISCAL PROBLEM.
Mr. W. Long and the Evils of
Protection.

Mr. William Long, J.P., presided over largely attended Liberal meeting held in the Congregational schools, Lymm, on Tuesday evening and delivered an' interesting speech on the all-absorbing fiscal question. He said the question before them was one that showed the importance men attached to that particular crisis in the history of Free Trade. It was that more than any- thing else that brought him out from the quiet seclu- sion of private life to take what little part he could in that cause. (Applause.) He felt that the people might he rather jumped upon by the perfect audacity of the proposals to do away with their great freedom in com- mercial matters. Still he could not understand how they seemed to be taken up by Mr. Chamberlain's pro- paganda. It was the audacity of the proposals which made the people listen. They. were carried away by his t. great energy and courage in taking up the position Rhich he had done, but he hoped the result would show that as English people they were not to be led away; and, much as they admired courage as Englishineu, they would think more of the welfare of the country. For himself he had no belief in the statements that had been made with reference to England's approaching ruin. The thing was perfectly monstrous, and, as one member of Parliament had said, ridicule was the best temper of mind in which to take the proposals. They knew, however, that Mr. Chamberlain had a great back- ing, especially amongst the nobility and the so-called higher class. When they looked at the composition of Mr. Chamberlain's audiences, or rather of all those about him on the platform at his meetings at Edinburgh and Glasgow, thoy could see they had motives of their own, but as to the working men, he could not under- stand what was to become of them. He was just old enough to know what' the effects of Protection were. He knew the labouring men's wages in the district of Lymm and Grappenhall were then 125., or at the most Hs., while at the present time the same men were getting from 18s.to 21s. a week. (Applause). Look at the cost of what they required, and compare it with the present cast, and they would find out what the differ- ence was. He could not understand why they (working men) could be caught by any cry that would lead them away from the blessings of freedom of commerce. He would not argue the question that night, bnt he would just like to ask his hearers to think who were the meu on the one side and who were the men on the other side. Further he would point to the fact that .amongst thel dissentients from the present policy of the Govern- ment there were four ex-Chancellors of the Exchequer. They were men of undoubted probity and high standing who had not seen fit to keep with the Government and had come out and left on account of the fiscal question (Applause). There was Sir William Harcourt, a man of great experience, and Lord Rosebery. (Applause). The latter gentleman had no interest in the question except the welfare of his country. (Hear, hear). He did not know whether it might be known to all of them, but he remembered the time when Mr. Gladstone and Mr. Cobden cleared off the last remaining vestige of Pro- tection, which removed taxes off something like 11,000 ao 12,000 articles. Would they (his hearers) like tog back to those days when they had to pay a tax on every little article they bought? They were too wide awake to believe that it was the exporter from the other countries who paid the taxes. Then they had another man on their side—a man of such calm judgment and great ascendency, he meant the Duke of Devonshire. (Loud applause). He had come forward at several crises in his country's history, once in a matter that took some of them away in 1888 when he left his party because he believed that the policylthat was likely' to be followed was against the best interests of the Empire Now he did the same thing, and had left the Govern- ment,solely and entirely upon the question of Free Trade. There was a point he would like to remark upon. Their opponents were very fond of saying that the Liberals , had no policy, that their Free Trade was a fetish, andl that they had better throw it over. One thing he was very much struck by was the suggestions of an old friend of theirs, Sir John Brunner. (Applause.) Sir:John was , a great friend not only to England but particularly to , his own district. Sir John said the Government ought to turn to and do something to promote the interests of trade and commerce in the country, and help educa- tion, and also prevent their great canals from • being bought up and monopolised. Concluding, he urged his hearers to stand by Free Trade. Protection would perhaps make the rich richer, but heavai quite positive it would make the poor poorer. (Loud ,applause.) Mr. W. J. Crossley, Liberal candidate for the Altrincham division, also spoke and a resolution con- demning the Government's policy and calling for an early dissolution was carried.

div.head: STRONG PROTECTIONIST VIEW.
div.p: A STRONG PROTECTIONIST VIEW.
" The End of England's Supremacy Very Near."
A FORMER WARRINGTONIAN'S OPINION.

Sir,—Will you oblige me with space to express some views on the Fiscal question which it appears to me in the endless discussion now going on escaped the atten- tion they should command? I will not indulge in statistics accessible to everyone in the speeches of our leading statesmen, in various able publications, and in endless local letters, nor willl occupy space to discuss 'he advantages of a cheap loaf, boots, hardware, and a ;housand other things achieved by the sacrifice of our ,wer to pay for anything. I wish simply to look at tr commercial history of the last fifty years, and, sing my anticipations of the future on the lessons of.

div.head: 311 1 T 1
div.p: er, Saturday December 19, 1903.
that period, to forecast what must of necessity follow in the near future if we continue the laissez faire policy so strenuously advocated by some of our leading statesmen.

--First, I may say free trade does not mean free im- ports, but free exchange of commodities. I presume 99 out of every 100 intelligent men believe in the former, and even Cobden himself would have repudi- ated the latter had he not been so far misled in his forecast of the future. I adopt implicitly every plank I in Mr. Chamberlain's platform, but disagree with him I in his conclusion that free trade, falsely so-called, ever was good for Great Britain, and more than ten years , ago I got a great snub from a leading statesman for , expressing the opinion that our Colonies were I useless to us except for the glory of appoint- ing a Governor-General, and high talk of the sun never setting',' on our "Dominion,' etc., unless we could establish some mutually beneficial trade arrangements, which, owing to the protective views then held by the commoners I thought impossible. Now, when I reversed the ordinary course of things and emigrated from Virginia to England nearly fifty years ago, ships from Liverpool were constantly arriv- ing in Norfolk where I lived, discharging railway iron, every ton of which was manufactured in England. The same applies to Manchester cotton goods, Yorkshire woollens, high-class machinery, cutlery, glass and china, tin plates, etc. I found England happy and prosperous with a population well nigh double what it is to-day, and politically content. Free imports could not then increase our exports, for we were the workshop of the world, and all other countries were under as pressing a necessity to take our manufactures as were the sons of Jacob to seek corn in Egypt. My deliberate opinion therefore is that we have in repealing all the duties done more for foreigners than merely prese.nt them with this tremendous sacrifice of revenue. In the repeal of the corn laws we have ruined our agricultural interests, the greatest we possess; we have reduced the value of real estate greater in amount than our national debt; we have rendered ourselves more hopelessly dependent on foreigners than ever for food, and thus increased the necessity for unlimited expenditure on our navy; we have created the Irish question ; we have expatriated the half of our rural population, and, having by this fiscal change rendered it necessary to pay the foreigner for food for our people, we have made him a present of millions of our adult population, and paid , all expenses of their emigration just when the ' human machine was in a position to re-pay I his cost in productive labour had such a thing I existed for him at home. That is to say, we I have paid the United States for rearing him, and delivered every adult so emigrating free at the spot where needed, when, according to the best estimates, we were adding at least £2OO to the national wealth of America in every adult transported. But this is not I all, or perhaps the worst, We have thus enormously increased the power of America to undermine our very national existence of which she is not slow to take I advantage. A cheap loaf may be a comforting hope to our tax-payers when the half of our populatioi . is in the workhouse or on foreign soil helping to sap the little work that is left •;is, but I apprehend our working population would prefer paying even a small increase in the cost of living with independence and good wages , ton workhouse or transportation. Now, with respect to our manufacturing interests, it would occupy too much space to go into statistics open to all in detail, but the arguments used by many of our leading statesmen in support of our free import policy fall unheeded on my mind, because I know them to be based ola false assumptions. Of course if it be accepted las axiomatic that under all conceivable circumstances to buy in the cheapest market is sound policy I would throw up the sponge, but does it help to the realization of the second popular maxim—viz., "sell in the dearest?" This has been the cry of the last sixty years, and has landed us in imports, I think, £180,000,000 in excess of our exports. No logic manufactured by man could ever convince me that this is evidence of pros- perity. I know as a matter of fact many of our indus- tries that were vigorous and money-making thirty years ago, and were then almost monopolised by England, have not increased, but rather gone back, though the consumption of the world has increased to at Ileast ten times what it u-as then. Germany and America have secured the whole increase and left us the small remnant that is so fiercely competed for that manufacturers keep their works open only to pay wages, and in the hope that i some change may occur n our fiscal policy or foreign methods that will redeem the situation. This relative decline I believe to be going on at an annual acceler- ating speed in every department of our industry, except in some highly exceptional localtrades, which in turn will suffer when our competitcirs are prepared for the attack. Now, all this is going on under the reign of an infallible sound fiscal policy. We the self-sacrificing adherents to sound principles, are decaying ,and America i and Germany, who ought to have gone into bankruptcy long ago, are going ahead by leaps and bounds. Surely the race has not yet died out "who would ruin the world for the sake of principle." Practical business men, however, view matters differently, and will not put a penny in new manufacturing works at home,and are investing their money abroad, while established manu- facturers, if able, are building works in foreign coun- tries, where they are not handicapped by injurious legislation, and are thus adding to the ruinous compe- tition that is swamping our prosperity. This increasing drain on our resources may go some way to explain the only plausible argument I see to support the assertion that we are now prospering viz., the increased return of income tax and invisible exports and imports. These appear to me unknown and unknowable, and I will not attempt to go into them; but one thing appears to me as 'clear as noonday sun—viz., that we are declining at an ever-accelerating speed, and if we do not effect some radical change on the lines advocated by Mr. Chamberlain—force fairer treatment from our competitors,or effect some mutually beneficial tariff arrangements with our colonies—the end of England's supremacy is very near, and our boasted national wealth will resolve itself into a sad memory of the past. Great numbers of people seem to. think that our national wealth under any conceivable condition is irreducible, and it is Mr. Asquith,l believe, who thinks that when our present industries fail this weilth may be conserved by manufacturers withdraw- ing their capital from obsolete works and creating new enterprises, and that our skilled artisans could relin- quish a craft they had spent seven years to learn and find profitable enployment in some unknown business yet to be discovered after our present industries are destroyed. I would remind all weak enough to indulge such hopes that our wealth does not consist in sovereigns but in reproductive work, railways, and all enterprises depending upon our commercial success for profit. A mill costing £lOO,OOO will be value for double that sum if it yields regularly 10 per cent. of dividend. Once de- monstrate that it can never make another dividend and its value, whatever it has cost, drops at once to that of scrap, and if that experience becomes general the wealth of England will at once disappear" as the base- less fabric of a vision." Elderly persons like many of our artisans may console themselves in the thought that" it will do our time," but for myself I feel that T would contemplate with sadness, even in a brighter world, the decay of England, and it is a deep sense of the frightful loss to the world such an event would bring that inspires the hope that God will take care of us if we fail to take care of ourselves —Yours &c.,
R. W. MURRAY.
Eaniskeen, Newcastle, County Dow-a: December 10th, 190.
[Many of our readers will doubtless recollect Mr. Robert Wallace Murray as one of the original founders of the Whitecross Company Limited.—ED,"

attendants were the first to enter. As Canada, Dora Payton wore a fur-trimmed costume which, of course reminded one of the severity of the winter in the dominion. She sweetly sang "The bird that leaves." Then there was a happy farmer (Percy Crampton) who rendered "Let the surplus populations," a lumberer (H. J. Iddon) with axe ready to fell the giants of the forest, a fully equipped hunter (William G. Smalley) and a typical fisherman (Percy Smith). A pleasing item was a trio by the lumberer, hunter and fisherman in which each:told of the joys of his particular calling. Two grimy miners (John Scragg and Thomas Lawton) sang 'Down the deep and dreary mine" in highly creditable style. As an Indian in full paint and feathers Arthur Bowers was a great success and his renderings of "Listen to the mocking bird" and "God save the King" in the native tongue called forth loud applause. A "Sleighing song" was rendered with fine spirit, the effect being heightened by the jingling of bells. The thoughts of the listeners were next directed to a warmer clime. The bright and picturesque garb of the Indians added another dash of colour to the scene. Florrie D.owns, as India, took her part well as, in fact, did all the performers. A detachment of Sepoys, clad in white suits and turbans, was composed of the following boys: H. Bairsto, E. Mather, C. Rigbey, H. Clement, L. White- 'house, J. Owen,R. Blackstock, W. T. Eccles, C, Billing- ton,M: Auckland, J. Peacock, A. Davies, and J. Rhoden. I A neigro was well portrayed by T. Parry, who gave a short song telling the story of the black man's slavery and its abolition. The British possessions in Africa next claimed the interest of the audience. The repre- sentation of Africa was entrusted to Mary Bather, who sang "From Europe's thick and foggy air "so effec- tively as to gain an encore, and her attendants included a farmer, waggon-driver, and Kaffir. Harry Hands made an admirable farmer and his sweet voice was heard to distinct advantage in I love the laud of the Southern Cross." H. Newall acquitted himself well as a waggon-driver,his song "When the morning mist" earning cordial approbation. The grotesque antics of the Kaffir (P. Egerton) created much amusement. A stirring chorus "To the East and the West" having I been rendered the Australian contingent entered. Alice Taylor, as Australia, sang and recited with marked con- fidence. Not less successful were T. Richmond (stock- man) and S. Jones (drover) whose "On theend less Australian plain "was vigorously and sweetl- interpreted and was greatly appreciated. Two ludicy rous characters were the blackman and his- gin (wife) and they could not have been placed in better hands. There was hearty laughter at the way in which W. Dunn and A. Dutton sustained these roles, the servility of the wife as she followed her lord and master adding much to the success of the representation. The song 'Black fellow he like plenty sheep "proved so popular that a repetition was insisted upon. The last colony from which Britannia received visitors was New Zealand, and the manner in which Ethel Cooper took the leading part left nothing to be desired. P. Ashcroft and H. Hewitt appeared as gold- diggers, carrying some of the implements used in the quest for the precious nuggets, and effectively rendered "With my little tin washing pan." There were also a dusky Maori chief with his wife A. Shakeshaft and R. Domville) who sang of the submission of the Maoris to the conquering English. Appropriate words of farewell and good-will were then spoken by Britannia and to the inspiriting strains of the chorus "Stretch forth! Stretch forth!" a general March past took place. The effect as in quick succes- sion the children in their vane-coloured costumes passed across the platform was almost kaleidoscopicand aroused the enthusiasm of the audience to a high pitch. Britannia and her attendants having made a stately I exit the first part of the entertainment was brought to ; a close. It should be mentioned that Master D. Daintith fulfilled the duties of lord-in-waiting with fitting ceremony. The choruses throughout the cantata I were given with accuracy and expression and the organ accompaniments were sinfully played by Mr. W. H. Payton, Mus. Bite., upon whom, in his capacity of music. ; master, much of the work of training the children had I devolved.

The second part of the programme, which was of a miscellaneous character, was equally enjoyable. A group of bop in sailor costume sang "The Powder Monkey," E. Wallington being responsible for the solo. The "hits" of the evening, however, were the sprightly selections from "The Geisha" and "San Toy" in which boys and girls figured with credit to themselves and their instructors. The popular "Chin-chin Chinaman" was rendered by the following boys in Chinese dress, whose gestures and dancing soon found them favour with the audience :—A. VVarburton, T. Bowcock, W. Aukland, T. Knowles, C. Short, T. Smith. The same boys also sang " Chinee sojee man" so well as to be vigorously recalled. The " Toy duet was admirably given by the following :—Boys: H. Hands, R. Olsson, H. Newall, T. Richmond, H. Cartwright, S. Jones. Girls: M. Routledge, E. Knowles, H. Bowcock, V. Dobson, M. Wilkinson and M. Grounds. The graceful dancing was a striking feature, and the audience would not be satisfied without a repetition of the item. Later the boys sang "What a beautiful world this would be" with gratifying success. " Six little wives" was another exceptionally meritorious contribution, in fact it is questionable whether a better rendering could have been given by children. As Yen How,Percy Crampton was quite at home, and the wives were impersonated in capital style by M. Atkinson, R. Dell, M. Ashley, J. Bond, E. Johnson and A. King. The concert concluded with the chorus "The River of Years." Before the last item was submitted

Mr. J. R. YOUNG, one of the school managers delivered a short speech. He pointed out that the old People's College Committee had, in consequence of the new Education Act, been disbanded, and they lost the services of several well-known veterans in the matter of education—men like Mr. Monks, Mr. J. J. Crosfield, who was for years their secretary, and Mr. Walter Milner, who for something like twenty years acted as treasurer. The old Committee which had watched over the interests of the institution zealously and lovingly for about half a century no longer existed. The school was now managed by a small committee consisting of four members of the old committee, and two gentlemen appointed by the local authority. He was extremely glad to be able to say that the two outsiders, if he might so term them were exceedingly capable men, anxious aud willing to further the interests of the institution, and when he told them that one of those gentlemen was perhaps better up in the Education Act than almost any man in Warrington it was a guarantee that they would continue to make the school prosper. Mr. Wallington desired him to draw attention to the photographs on the pro- gramme of, 201 boys and girls who had, for twelve months, not missed a single attendance. To his mind, and to the mind of any ordinary individual, that was a gigantic triumph, but Mr. Wallington thought they might do much better. It was well to know that the progress in this direction had been great, for four years ago there were only sixteen scholars who had attained the distinction. Last year the number was 175 and now it had made a further gratifying advance. This meant that there were some hundreds of parents in War- rington who understood the advantages of punctuality but over and above that fact it was well to remember that every time a child failed to attend school it was a positive cost to the town of a fraction over a penny. The total number of absences from all the schools in Warrington brought up the total cost to something like twopence or threepence in the £ so that there was really something worth trying for in regular attendance. Mr. Young proceeded to congratulate Mr. Payton, the teachers and scholars upon the magnificent success of the concert and specially mentioned Miss Clarke, Miss Brown and Mr. Bowen upon whom much of the work had devolved. In conclusion he thanked the parents for their co-operation and the audience for their attendance.

div.head: PEOPLE'S COLLEGE CONCERT.
div.p: PEOPLE'S COLLEGE CONCERT.
A Patriotic Cantata at tha Parr Hall.

Escaping from the murky atmosphere of the streets on Thursday evening, it was indeed a pleasant relief to enter thell'arrliall where there was refreshing brightness and animation. Three hundred and fifty children in all the glory of fine raiment, with faces glowing with pleasure and enthusiasm, occupied the spacious plat- form 'gallery and the hall was filled with a vast audience attractedby the well-earned reputation of People'sColle.e concerts. It was nome,an tabute to the success which has attended the efforts of the teachers and scholars to provide entertainments in the past that so many of the townspeople should be desirous of wit- nessing this -the fourth of the new series of annual concerts. Not a seat was unoccupied and taking a general survey of the hall, a veritable sea of faces inet one's, gaze. It is a pleAstire to be able to j congratulate all concerned in the promotion of the concert upon the abundant fruit—in the form of com- plete and signal success—which . their labours have borne. The work of preparation was willingly Under- taken but it must be a source of unfeigned gratification to teachers and scholars alike that the geaeral public rally round them and, by attendance and cordially ex- pressed appreciation,afford them every encouragement. Thursday's concert was on different lines from any of the three which have preceded it, the major portion of the long and interesting programme consisting of T. Mee Pat tison's cantata Britannia and her daughters." The work, of course, appeals to patriotic sentiment and serves to bring home to one's mind the bond of union which exists between the mother country and her colonies and dependencies beyond the seas. Enthroned in regal splendour ' Britannia receives representatives of distant races who own her sway and are anxious to do homage lind offer assurances of unswerving loyalty. To Miss Annie Clarke the important part of Britannia wasallotted,and she com- ported herself with becoming dignity. While the organ pealed forth triumphal strains she was escorted to the throne with due pomp and ceremony and around her a band of small but sturdy bluejackets stood guard. The effect. was pretty in the extreme. Britannia, dressed in flowing white robes, with shining helmet and trident, having assumed her exalted position the chorus" Mighty Britannia! Mother of 1 Nations!" swelled front 350 youthful throats. As the cantata progressed,it could be seen that the mere learning of it must in itself have been an admirable lesson to the children in the geography, climate, and productions of the British dominions. The representatives of each land were clad in typical cos- tumes and having made obeisance to Britannia they sang"and spoke of the advantages of their.country, and afterwards received a kindly greeting. div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
Rugby Football. By " Ovalist."

Warrington were in the fog once more on Satur- day, and as most people expected they succumbed to Leeds on the Headingley ground. The condition of things in Lancashire was excellent from a football point of view, but the broad acres of the neighbouring county were almost hidden in mist. The game at Leeds was only occasionally visible to the crowd, -and even then it was not very exhilarating. There was no score until near the close of play, when Llewellyn scored a try for the,hotne team which proved to be the winning point.

Those people who went with the Warrington team came back somewhat disgusted, for their favourites had by no means played up to form. There was a lack of earnestness and determination on the part of the players which precluded • them from winning by anything but the most lucky chance. Tha forwards were far more badly beaten than they should have been, and it was freely said that the men looked upin the result as a foregone conclusion, and consequently did not exert themselves. They had nothing very much to fight against but weight and strength on Satur- day, and a little determination might have turned the scale. Leeds are, however, a fine forward team, and they kept Warrington mostly on the defensive. It really looked as if the defence was going to prevail until the fog lifted ten minutes from the close, and the Leeds men got a glimpse.of the line.

Hallam and Hockenhall were easily the best of the Warrington backs, the remainder of whom were seen to little advantage. Fish was very lackadaisical and quite failed to uphold the reputation he established at Leeds in the first round of the cup-ties during War- rington's most successful year. The full back de- lighted everyone, and there is no questioning tho fact that Hallam just now is with the very front rank of Northern Union custodians.
It has been made evident of late that Warrington require more weight in the scrummage. The present

I fancy the want of a crack half back would not be felt so keenly were the forwards only capable of holding their own anywhere, for Davies, - Mahoney and Bate, can all give a creditable display behind the scrum- mage. Additional forward streegth is be ng eagerly sought and there is ground for expecting new blood before very long. In the meantime, the men doing duty have gat to show a little more " bant "or look- out for squalls.

There has never been a more keenly fought com- petition under the Northern Union than that for the senior league championship this season. Even now there are only two points between the first half-dozen clubs and nearly every week that passes brings a change in the leadership. Oldham had a fine prospect up to last Saturday when they came an awful cropper before the dispised of Widnes, and on the Water- sheddings ground too. The Chemicals though five points behind at half-time won in the end by 9 points to 8 points, and the faces of the Oldhamers were beyond description. Such a shock has not been felt in Spindledom ::or many years and advice to the com-. mittee and players just now is:plentif ul and gratuitous. Bravo, Widnes ! say I. There's nothing like trying. Warrington please note !
, Leeds have made a big advance and are now level with the leaders. The table up to date is as follows :

• Warrington "\. "have been under a cloud of late, but they came out in a blaze of glory on Saturday. True, the opposition was only Widnes Rangers, but it was the really fine form of the home backs which resulted in a score of 4 goals 11 tries (41 points) to nil. The c ombination was as good as anything seen on the ground this season. Duckworth and Mahoney made abig difference to the side, which was effective all round except at full back, where Jordan was not the equal of Tom Knight. But then he was not expected to be a Bancroft or Winfield all at once.

One man deserves a par all to himself, and that man is Kenyon, the new left-winger. He ,fairly "staggered humanity" on Saturday by running in no less than. seven tries, And thereby, I believe, establishing a record for the Warrington club. Why even Jack Fish never obtained more than five tries in an afternoon! There is something out of the common in a youngster who 'does this sort of thing, and Kenyon certainly proved himself possessed of speed and scoring ability. He is a well-built lad, too, and the way he went for the line was an education to some of the men who have been tried in the same position. • What he lacks is of course, experience,and When he has gained that he should be a valuable acquisition to the Warrington ranks. A man who can score is badly needed.

The Lancashire Combination table up-to-date is as follows .

Runcorn are to be the visitors to Warrington to-day, and as mulch interest is being shown in the match as ever there was. Warrington have a lot of lee-way to make up before they can look back upon the record of Runcorn engagements with anything like satisfaction. The "Linnets " have had the best of matters for a long time, though the last two year's has seen some levelling up, and Warrington have gained a point or two. ,Last season, however, Run- corn made a pointless draw at Warrington, and whacked the Warrington men by IS points to nil at Irwell-lane, so that a big effort is called for from the Wilderspool brigade to-day. The match will also count in the South-West Lancashire Competition, and with four points depending on the issue, Warrington must 'make no mistake.

The Warrington team will be :—Hallam, full hack ; Fish, Isherwood, Dickenson, and Hookenhpll, three- quarters; • Davies and Bate, half-backs ; Boardman, Morrison, Thomas, Cook, Edmondson, Naylor, Swift. and Jolley, forwards. Runcorn are now at full strength again, as was evident by the way they trounced Leigh on Saturday. Their weakest point is forward, and there is a chance here for the Warrington eight to manifest their superiority in such a way as to leave no doubt about the ultimate issue.

The "A" team will be fully extended at Runcorn, but on last Saturday's form they should give a good account of themselves. The chosen twelve are: Knight, full-back; Kenyon, Mahoney,and Short, three- quarters; Duckworth and Edmunds, half-backs; bunt, Harmer, Warburton, Forster, Woods, and Swift, forwards. .

A Northern Union International match has been arranged for New, Year's Day at Oldham, and two strong teams are picked. Fish is, of course, on the left wing for" England " and Thomas is reserve for- ward for " other nationalities." The Warrington committee are asking that both men be released as Warrington have an important South West Lancashire fixture with St Helens on New Year's Day. It will probably be new to most of my readers to learn that this match will count four points in the competition as St. Helens only meet their rivals, who are all in the. senior league, once this season. Four points are at stake on each match, and the saints are going to fight hard for them. Warrington do not wish- to have their chance of ultimate honours pre- judiced by the loss of Fish and Thomas for the St. Helens match, especially as the international game is merely a friendly encounter and or no importancz...

div.head: GRAPPENHALL
div.p: GRAPPENHALL

CONCERT.—On Wednesday evening last, a grand concert was held in the Large Room at Grappenhall, in connection with the Grappenhall St. Wilfrid's Cricket Club. Songs were given by the following artistes, viz., Miss Carrie Hastings. Miss L. Fairhurst, 1 Mr. A. Green- hough, Mr. Percy George, and The Apollo Male Voice Quartette, who were well applauderblor their numerous songs. Violin solos were excellently played by Mr. Tom Boothroyd. The humorous element was supplied by Mr. Arthur G. Davies, of Liverpool, who caused much laughter with his different sketches. The accom- panists were Mr. T. Brough and Mr. A. E, Trow.

The ;Examiner, Satur3a7, December 19, 1903 A VETERAN WARRINGTON ORGANIST. Presentation to Mr. Thomas Mather. Tnere was an interesting gathering in St. Mary's School, I3uttermarket-street, Warrington, on Monday evening, when a presentation was made to Mr. Thomas Mather, who has recently resigned the position of organist and choirmarter of St. Mary's Church, a position he has occupied since the church was erected. A musical programme was provided by members of the choir, and the proceedings were attended by a large number of friends who were desirous of showing their appreciation of Mr. Mather's long services. The presen- tation consisted of a handsome rose bowl and an illu- minated address, subscribed to by the clergy, choir and friends. After the first part of the musical programme had been submitted, the presentation was made. The Rev.. Father Wilson, 0.5.8., presided and he was accompanied on the platform by the Rev. Father Mercer,D.D., 0.5.8. Mr. Thomas Mather, Messrs. A. Boyle, James Boyle, W Kilduff, .L Eckersley, W. Dilworth, J. Bannon and J. Bradley. • The Rev. Father Wfasos observed that 'pleasant as had been the items of the programme they had already listened to, he thought, without any reflection on the artistes, he might say they had now come to the most gratifying item of all. (Hear, hear). The very centre and object of that evening's gathering was to do honour to Mr. Mather. (Applause.) He would ask the secre- tary of the presentation committee to read the address and read letters of apology. Mr. A. Boyle then read communications from Mr. Richard Eccles and Mr. Langley, anologising for their' absence. The illurninatedaddress, he continued read as follows :—" To Mr: Thomas Mather. We, the under- signed desire on your retirement from the position of organist and director of the choir at St. Mary's to record our hearty recognition of your very long and valuable services. Before St. Mary's Church was built , yon devoted your art and energies for manyj years to the only Catholic Church in the town (Applause.) From the opening of St. Mary's Church 26 years ago you have discharged with honour and success the duties from which you now retire. It is impossible here to recount the varied achievements of those long years of self-sacrifice and labour. Let it suffice to say that it has been to you always a labour of love—love of your church and love of your art. Of this however, we can assure you that you have established for yourself in that long lapse of time a place for the grateful and kindly remembrances of those who have been associated with you in the choir and of a multitude of others,both clergy and laity, fr 2 m which you will never be permitted to retire while fife lasts.(Applause.)This mall token of appreciation! and gratitude we beg you to accept with our hearts' best wishes for still longer years of health and happiness." The address was signed by the follow ing clergy and members of the choir :—Neville Wilson- Peter Mercer, R. B. Primavesi, J. Eckersley, William, Kilduff, Alban Boyle, John Bannon, M. G. Hearne, Agatha Richardson, Sabina Mannion Fannie Hayes, ' Agnes Mather, Kate Brown* Agnes E. Richardson, Peter Langley, James Boyle, William Dilworth, Austin Perron, F. Magian, and Joseph Bradley. The Rev. Father Wiasox then formally handed the presents to Mr. Mather amid hearty applause. The address which had just been read to them, the Chairman continued, expressed in some measure their thoughts and feelings towards Mr. Mather. (Hear, hear.) ft did not contain all they thought or felt or perhaps all they would like to say. That would be impossible on such an address, but it was one which he hoped Mr Mather would keep and be honourably proud of for many years to come. (Hear, hear.) He (the Chairman) was not qualified to go through the musical career of Mr. Mather. To those in Warrington he supposed Mr. Mather was almost the embodiment of history, ancient and modern—(laughter)—whereas he (the Chairman) came upon the acene only very recently—as of yesterday really compared with Mr. :Mather's 26 long years of service to St. Mary's, besides a period of service— he did not know of what duration befere,—to St. Alban's. They were there to give honour to whom honour was due. (Hear, hear.) The man who had conducted a choir, and managed it and the organ for 26 years without any serious contretemps—for that would be a serious matter in music—deserved congratu- lation and honour. (Hear, hear.) They did 'well to recognize the services of those who had given their skill and their energy to the service of God's church. Music was one of those things that went to make up the beauty of the sanctuary and the church would be at least for us a very dull place comparatively, if we had not amongst the other aids to religion that of music. The inscription which was engraven on the bowl was as follows: "A token of esteem. Presented on his retire- ment to Mr. Mather, 26 years organist of St. Mary's by the choir and many other friends. December, 1903." He had a word to say about this rose bowl. When the committee was engaged in selecting the article, he found out, what he daresay most of them knew very well, but on such matters he supposed he was particu- larly innocent. (Laughter.) The article' he found out was not at all the harmless and innocent thing it looked to be. (Laughter.) This rose bowl looked a very inno- cent thing with the netting on top of it, but he ascer- tained that it could sometimes contain a fragrance quite other than that of roses and which had nothing what- ever to do with flowers. (Laughter.) He found if he might aciapt a line of Goldsmith'sto the circumstances, it was an article contrived a double debt to pay 'a bowl for punch at night and flowers by day." (Laugh- ter.) The secret was out. (Loud laughter.) He did not intend to say that in the presenca of Mr. Mather. He did not suppose Mr. Mather would ever have found it out for himself. (Laughter.) But whether it!was used by day or night.be hoped that to Mr. Mather itwould always contain the nectar of sweet and pleasant remembrances. The Rev. Father MERCER facetiously observed that after the confession of particular innocence on the part of Father Wilson that there was little for him to say. (Laughter.) He thought the large attendance at that meeting was in itself a great tribute to Mr. Mather's worth, :tad one which he hoped Mr. Mather would highly appreciate. It showed the effect of that kindly spirit of his all through the years that he had worked in har- mony with everyone. (Hear, hear.) The presentation was only a small token of the feelings they had towards Mr. Mather, <Oar) came to St. Mary's from the mother church at St. Alban's 26 years ago, and had been respon- sible for the musical portion of the services ever since. He heartily joined in the expression of appreciation of Mr. 'Mather's services. Mr. W. KILDUFF, speaking as one of the oldest members of the choir, referred to Mr. Mather's vigour and enthusiasm for church music. It was a great re- spansibility for anyone to undertake the management of a mixed choir. but Mr. Mather had succeeded both at St. Mary's and St. Alban's, his term of conductor- ship extending over thirtyyears. He remembered Mr. Mather in the days when Father Hall went round for his pennies with the object of building a grand Roman Catholic Church in Warrington, which was almost to approach aCatbedral. (He.ar,hear.) He hoped it would do some day. In addition to his work in connection with the church, Mr. Mather was one of the prime movers in connection with the late St. Alban's Drama- tic Society, the Catholic Philanthropic Society, and the Cristy Minstrel troupe. (Hear ,hear.) Mr. J. BOYLE said he had been called upon to speak as a member of the choirs of St. Alban's and St. Mary's. Mr. Langley was also a member of both choirs and it would have been his place to speak if he had been present. He remembered Mr. Mather before he com- menced playing the organ at St. Alban's. He believed Mr. Mather succeeded his uncle, Mr. Kaye at the organ over thirty years ago. (Hear, hear). During that long period Mr. Mather had continuously given of his mus- ical ability for the benefit of the Catholic church. He hoped Mr. Mather would have prosperity to the end of his days. (Hear, hear). Mr. A. BOYLE said they were making a presentation to a gentlemantwho was worthy of it. Mr. Mather had worked energetically for the promotion of music in the Catholic churches in the town. Some of the finest church music produced in the district had been given at St. Mary's church. Mr. Mather was not only respected by his Catholic -friends but also by many Protestant friends, some of whom were present to show their respect. Mr. MATHER, who on rising to acknowledge the gift, was received with the singing of "He's a jolly good fellow," and cheers, said he, had appeared in that room many times, but he had never gone through an ordeal such as that. (Applause.) If they put his years of service as organist of St. Alban's and St. Mary's together they totalled up to 35 years. (Applause.) He slice 3eded his uncle, Mr. Kaye who was organist for 41 years—(hear, hear,)—and he thought that was not a bad record for two members of one family. He did not say it in a boasting spiriti He was only too proud to have been permitted to work ' so long for. the Benedictine Order. (Applause.) He was not the only one, others were equally deserving of praise. He remembered one of the priests telling him that everybody had three evils to contend 'with—the devil, the world and the flesh—but that priests had thfee others—school teachers, organists and choirs. (Loud laughter.) He (Mr. Mather) did not know what the experience of other organists and choir masters had been, but during his long experience he had never had any serious difficulty in Warrington. They had always sailed along very pleasantly at St. Mary's, and during his long experience he could not recall any serious dis- agreement. He was thankful that he had been given such good health, for during the first 30 years he had not missed six Sunday morning services. Latterly his health had not been so good, but he had always been able to rely on Mr. Eckersley on occasions when he was absent. He, wished specially to thank the lady members of the Lihoir for their assistance. Referring to Father Wilson's allusion to the double use to which the bowl could be put, Mr. Mather said if anything else but roses were put into the bowl he hoped it would be`Melrose.' ' The musical programme was then continued. Two choruses were given by the choir with feeling and expression' namely "The Angelus" from " Maritana " and "The Soldiers Chorus " from "Faust." Miss F. Hayes was heard to advantage in " Dear Heart," and Miss Agatha Richardson very sweetly sang "Oh dry those tears."' Messrs. Joseph and Peter Bate sang with effect the duet " Flow gentle Deva." Mr. W. Kilduff contributed a humorous song entitled "Early in the morning," and solos were also very efficiently sung by Mr. John Rabbit, Mr. John Bannon. and Mr. John Gibbins, Mr. J. NV. McAvoy who performed the duties of accompanist also played a pianoforte solo.

SIX MONTHS' FATALITIES. An official return shows that during the six months ending June 30, 1903, four persons were killed and 368 injured in accidents to trains, rolling stock, permanent way, &c., in the United Kingdom. The figures for the corresponding period in 1902 were five killed and 408 injured. The total number of casualties of all kinds in the course of public traffic in the six months was 569 killed and 3,079 injured. The total includes suicides and accidents at level crossings.

Post free 12 stamps. floldroyd's Medical A meeting of this Council will be held in the Town Hall on Monday evening. THE USE OF SCHOOLS AFTER SCHOOL HOURS. db. AA. In accdrdance with the decision of the Education Committee at their last meeting, the Finance Com- mittee re-considered their resolution with reference to the use of schools after school hours by the teachers, and' after discussion, it was resolved that the com- mittee will remit the charge to the managers in respect of the use of school rooms for purposes of an educa- tional character, when such use is continuous with an ordinary school meeting, and is limited to scholars on the school registers, provided that the managerssatisfy the committee as to the reasonableness of the fees charged. SCHOOL KEEPERS DUTIES. The Finance Committee also reconsidered their resolu- tion which was referred back to the committee by the Education Committee at their last meeting by the Education Committee at their last meeting, with refer- ence to the request of the managers of the Wycliffe British school that the school keeper may be allowed to retain the office of keeper of the Church, and had an interview with the correspondent of the managers of the school (Mr. P. T. Winskill) on behalf of the managers. After careful consideration, it was resolved that the committee re-affirms its previous decision that they cannot accede to the request. THE EDUCATION OFFICES. A letter was submitted to the Finance Committee from the Town Clerk, intimating that the Finance and Estate Committee would be prepared to rent the Old Vicarage in Sankey-street to the committee for use as an office, for the stun of £5O per annum, and it was re- solved that the premises in question be rented on the terms set out in the letter. THE INSURANCE OF SCHOOL FURNITURE. A letter was submitted to the Finance uommittee from the Association of foundation managers of the Church of England schools, requesting the Committee to arrange for the insurance of the school furniture against fire, and it was resolved, that a scheme for the insurance of thelfurniture in the schools, including pro- vision for an equitable arrangement forth° payment of propostion of the cost thereof by the Managers, be drawn up for the consideration of the Committee. AN ADDITIONAL AT TENDANCE OFFICER, WiThe School attendance Committee recommend that an additional School Attendance Officer be appointed at a commencing salary or £65 rising to a maximum of .C9l per annum. At a later meeting it was resolved that Mr. William Farrar and Mr. Thomas William Holbrook be appointed school attendance officers, at a commenc- ing salary, in each cas.e. of £65 per annum: the engage- ments dating from the 30th November, 1003, and being determinable by one month's notice, to expire on the last day of any calendar month, given by or to the Com- mittee. THE QUESTION OF "FAIR WEAR AND TEAR:, The Sites and Buildings Committee cansidered the best means of dealing with the question of fair wear and tear in the various elementary schools in the Borough, and the proportion of the cost in respect thereof to be borne by the Education Committee, and, after some discussion, it was resolved that, pending the receipt of the report of the Borough Surveyor on the condition of the school buildings, the matter be deferred for consideration by the committe3 at a special meet- ing to be held for the purpose. PROPOSED NEW SCHOOLS. At the meeting of the Sites and Building Committee the Chairman reported the result of the sub-com- mittee's efforts to secure sites for the new schools to be erected in Latchford and Cockhedge, and it was resolved that the Director confer with H.M. Inspector as to the desirability of certain sites. The following recommendation of the School Attendance Committee was submitted and noted, viz. :—" That the plans for the proposed new school in Latchford should be pre- pared so that, if necessary, an extension could be made of the Boys' department to increase the accommodation to 300." PLANS OF SCHOOLS. It was resolved by the Sites and Buildings Committee that a survey be made and plans of the schools prepared by the Borough Surveyor, and that he be authorised ro obtain additional assistance for this purpose. A LUMINOUS TREE. A most remarkable luminous tree grows in Brazil. it is about six or seven feet in height, and is so luminous that it can be plainly distinguished in the darkest night for a distance of more than a mile, while in its imme - diate vicinity it emits sufficient light toenable a person to rend very fine print. WANTED TO GET BACK TO SIBERIA. Mr. Lowe, K.C., asked Mr. Justice Darling on Monday to expedite the hearing of a case on the ground that some of the witnesses were here from Siberia, and were anxious to return. His lordship said it was the first time he had ever heard of people who had got away from Siberia being anxious to go back again, but he would endeavour to meet their wishes. MARKET INSPECTOR'S NEW APPOINTMENT. Mr. William Garrett, Runcorn Market Inspector, has been appointed Inspector of the Shrewsbury Market. He commenced his new duties on Monday.

' The third annual meeting of the Warrington and District Branch of the aly-)ve association was held in the old school attendance offices Sankev-street, War- rington, on Saturday.—ln the absence of the President (Mr. W. Jones) through illness, and the Vice-Presi- dent, the chair was occupied by Mr. T. Bromilow (St. Helens).—The Secretary (Mr. W. Rutter) read his annual report from which it appeared that two meet- ings had been held during the year,one at Warrington in February, and the other at Runcorn in May, both meetings 'being well attended and successful. The meeting arranged for August was abandoned owing to the midsummer holidays being on at that time. The balance sheet was presented and showed a loss on the year's working, but there is still a balance in hand to commence the year with. The following officials were elected for the ensuing year, viz : President, Mr. W. Jones, Warrington; Vice-President, Mr. T. Martindale, Earlestown ; Secretary and Trea- surer, Mr. W. Rutter, Warrington; Committee, Messrs. T. Bromilow, St. Helens, G. Howard, Runcorn ; 0. Davies, Widnes ; W. Bamber, Warrington and J. If. Att. "RITA" .AND THE SMART SET. "Rita," summing up her charges against "smart" society in this week's Gentlewoman," emphasises the need of "a very strong hand" to'overthrow "the temple of smartness," and continues :—What do we owe the " smart " set? The introduction of nameless follies. the effrontery of shamelessly lived lives, the wanton extravagance of men and women who cry " thief " to the poor outcast who picks up a handkerchief they drop, a card case they mislay, and yet think it no dis- honour to rob tradesmen, to run up accounts they are quite unable, and still more unwilling, to pay ! The nation's salvation, she declares, is to come from "the steady brain and sterling commonsense of her middle- class."
